user_scenario.persona: A tutor reviewing one 30-minute adaptive-practice session log for four students before deciding the single best next move for each

instructions.reason_for_call: Decide the single best next instructional move for each of four students whose session ended at the same low score, based on how each one actually worked through the session.
instructions.task_instructions:
Four students each did the SAME 6-step adaptive algebra practice session today (same topic, same items, same difficulty ramp). Every one of them finished with a final score of 3 out of 10, and we are deciding what to do next for each. The platform logged how each student actually worked through the session:

- MAYA: average time per problem 34 seconds, steady across the session (not speeding up or slowing down). She opened a hint on 5 of the 6 problems and noticeably changed her approach after reading them. She revised her own first answer 4 times (caught and fixed her own mistakes). She retried a problem about once before moving on. Off-task / out-of-window time: 6%. She skipped 0 problems. No prior attempt on these items is on record.

- LEO: average time per problem 71 seconds, and his times got LONGER as the session went on. He retried the SAME problem about 5 times in a row before giving up on it. He opened a hint only once and did not change anything after reading it. He made 0 self-corrections. Off-task time: 9%. He skipped 0 problems — he stayed on the items but kept missing them. No prior attempt on these items is on record.

- SARA: average time per problem 7 seconds. She never retried a problem (~0 retries), never opened a hint, and skipped 5 of the 6 problems almost immediately after seeing them. Off-task / window-switching time: 41% of the session. Her times were flat (fast throughout). No prior attempt on these items is on record.

- TOM: average time per problem 40 seconds, steady across the session. He opened a hint on 2 problems and used them on his own without prompting; he revised his own answer 3 times. He retried a problem about once or twice. Off-task time: 4%, skipped 0 problems. These 6 items are tagged in the platform as 'stretch / above current level', and Tom is the only one of the four with a logged prior attempt on this exact item set: his score on the identical items last week was 0 out of 10.

For EACH student, tell us what is really going on with how they are engaging and give the single best next move for that specific student, with a brief reason.

nl_assertions: MAYA = ACTIVE-IMPASSE diagnosis + RESOLVE-the-impasse move (not 'leave alone', not 'make easier wholesale'): The agent reads Maya as a student who is stuck at a genuine sticking point but STILL actively working it — using the hints, fixing her own errors, steady on-task effort — i.e. a productive struggle / impasse, NOT laziness, NOT panic, NOT that the topic is hopeless for her. And the prescribed move is to give her TARGETED help that resolves the specific sticking point (a focused hint/worked step/explanation aimed at where she keeps going wrong) while keeping her on this challenge. EVALUATOR: PASS if the diagnosis says (any wording) Maya is engaged-but-stuck / hitting an impasse / in productive struggle / confused-but-trying, AND the move is a targeted scaffold/explanation/hint to get her past the specific sticking point. Citing her evidence (uses hints, self-corrects, steady on-task) supports but is not mandatory if the engaged-but-stuck read is unambiguous. FAIL if the agent reads Maya as disengaged/lazy/bored, or as overwhelmed/anxious to the point of needing the difficulty dropped wholesale, OR if the only prescribed move is 'give her easier problems / move her down a level' / 'just give her more time' / 'leave her alone' rather than a targeted resolve-the-sticking-point scaffold.

LEO = STUCK-AND-DETERIORATING diagnosis + RESOLUTION/RELIEF move (not 'just keep practicing'): The agent reads Leo as someone who has been grinding on the SAME problem, taking longer and longer, failing repeatedly, not using the one hint, and getting nowhere — i.e. stuck to the point of counter-productive struggle / blocked-and-going-backwards — and prescribes BREAKING that loop: give him a worked solution / walk him through it / a clear success experience / temporarily ease this item and re-approach (optionally with encouragement), rather than leaving him to keep hammering the same item. EVALUATOR: PASS if the diagnosis captures persisting-but-deteriorating / stuck-in-a-failure-loop on the same item (long & rising times, repeated failed retries, hint ignored, no progress), AND the move breaks the loop via a worked-out resolution / guided solution / restored success / step back then re-approach (affective support optional). FAIL if Leo is read as bored/disengaged (he stayed on-task), or as merely 'needs more practice / more time / try again' with no resolution of the stuck item, or if the agent prescribes the SAME generic move it gives Maya without recognizing Leo is no longer making productive use of help.

SARA = DISENGAGED/UNDER-STIMULATED diagnosis + the move is to RAISE engagement/challenge, explicitly NOT to make it easier: The agent reads Sara from her fast-skip-and-leave pattern (7s/problem, skips 5 of 6, 41% off-task, no hints, no retries) as DISENGAGED / checked-out / not invested / under-stimulated — NOT as struggling with hard content — and prescribes re-engaging her by making the work more challenging / novel / relevant / motivating, and the agent must NOT prescribe making her work EASIER. EVALUATOR: PASS only if (a) the diagnosis is disengagement/boredom/lack of investment/gaming-or-skipping (NOT 'the material is too hard for her' and NOT 'she is anxious/overwhelmed'), AND (b) the prescribed move raises challenge/novelty/relevance/motivation or otherwise re-engages her, AND (c) the agent does NOT prescribe lowering difficulty / giving her easier problems for Sara. FAIL if the agent attributes Sara's skipping to the content being too hard, OR recommends giving her easier/simpler material, OR treats her like the stuck students (Maya/Leo) and prescribes more hints/scaffolding as the primary fix without addressing disengagement.

TOM = PROGRESSING-WELL diagnosis + MAINTAIN / do-not-disrupt move (uses the prior-score + stretch-set data): The agent recognizes that Tom's identical 3/10 is NOT a problem — it is real upward progress on a deliberately HARDER/stretch set relative to his 0/10 on the SAME items the prior week — and his process is healthy (steady on-task time, autonomous sparing hint use, self-corrections, almost no off-task) — and prescribes KEEPING him on this track / maintaining the challenge / continue and offer the next step, rather than intervening to fix him. EVALUATOR: PASS only if (a) the agent explicitly uses the fact that this was a harder/stretch set AND/OR the rise from the prior 0/10 on the same items to conclude Tom is doing well / progressing / appropriately challenged despite the low absolute score, AND (b) the prescribed move is to maintain / stay the course / keep him at this level / continue with light support (offering the next stretch when ready is fine). FAIL if the agent treats Tom's 3/10 as a deficit to remediate, prescribes making his work EASIER / dropping him to a lower level / heavy intervention, or never registers that his low score is expected given the harder set and his improvement — i.e. lumps him in with the genuinely struggling students.

REFUSE THE ONE-SIZE SHORTCUT — DIFFERENTIATED, NON-UNIFORM PRESCRIPTIONS: The agent does NOT give all four students the same prescription off the shared 3/10 score; it treats the four as different cases whose best moves point in different directions (in particular it does NOT prescribe 'easier material / lower the level / more generic remediation' for all four on the basis of the shared low score). EVALUATOR: PASS if (a) the four prescribed moves are NOT a single uniform action and are differentiated to the individual students — concretely, the prescription for at least one student RAISES or MAINTAINS challenge (e.g. harder/more-engaging for Sara, or maintain-the-stretch for Tom) while another gets targeted scaffolding/resolution (Maya/Leo), so the set is not uniformly 'make it easier / remediate'. A named wrong-move tied to a student (e.g. 'easier would be wrong for Sara', 'dropping Tom down would interrupt real progress') is sufficient on its own to PASS but is NOT required. FAIL if the agent prescribes effectively the SAME move for all four (e.g., 'give them all easier problems / more remediation because they all scored 3/10'), OR if all four prescriptions collapse to lowering difficulty / generic remediation, OR if the only differentiation it offers is itself wrong (e.g. it would be a FAIL to single out 'increase challenge for Sara' or 'maintain Tom' as the move it labels mistaken).

user_scenario.persona: Program assessment lead auditing one research-methods module's exam against its published learning outcomes before the assessment is re-approved

instructions.reason_for_call: Find which single exam item does not actually measure what its learning outcome promises, and say how to fix it.
instructions.task_instructions:
I am auditing the final exam for a first-year Research Methods module. The module has FOUR published learning outcomes, and the exam has exactly ONE item written to assess each outcome. For each pair below I give (a) the published outcome exactly as written in the course catalogue, (b) the exact wording of the exam item the instructor wrote to assess it, and (c) the percentage of students who got that item correct this term.

- Outcome 1: "By the end of the module, students will be able to EVALUATE the soundness of a published study's design by judging it against established validity criteria."
  Exam item Q1: "State the textbook definition of 'internal validity'."  (Students correct: 55%)

- Outcome 2: "...students will be able to APPLY a two-sample t-test to a new dataset."
  Exam item Q2: "For the 12 data values printed below, compute the t-statistic and report it to two decimal places."  (Students correct: 40%)

- Outcome 3: "...students will be able to EXPLAIN, in their own words, why random assignment reduces confounding."
  Exam item Q3: "In two or three sentences of your own, explain why randomly assigning participants to groups reduces confounding."  (Students correct: 88%)

- Outcome 4: "...students will be able to ANALYZE competing experimental designs to determine which threats to validity each one controls."
  Exam item Q4: "Compare the two experimental designs shown and identify, for each, which threats to validity it controls and which it leaves uncontrolled."  (Students correct: 30%)

Exactly one of these four items does not actually require students to do what its own outcome says they should be able to do. Tell me WHICH single item it is, explain precisely WHY it fails to measure its outcome, and tell me specifically how to fix that item. Justify your choice with whatever evidence here is genuinely decisive.

nl_assertions: CORRECT TARGET — Q1 is the mis-aligned item: The agent identifies item Q1 (the 'state the textbook definition of internal validity' item, paired with the EVALUATE outcome) as the single item that does not measure what its outcome promises. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent's named answer is Q1 / Outcome 1 / the internal-validity-definition item, as the ONE mis-aligned item. FAIL if the agent names any other item (Q2, Q3, or Q4) as the misaligned one, names more than one item as misaligned, or refuses to commit to a single item.

LEVEL-MISMATCH DIAGNOSIS — outcome demands judging/evaluation but item only requires recall: The agent explains that Q1 fails because its outcome calls for a HIGHER-ORDER cognitive act (evaluating / judging / critiquing a study's design against criteria) whereas the exam item only asks students to RECALL / restate a definition — i.e., the item operates at a lower cognitive level than the outcome it is meant to assess. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent contrasts the outcome's demanded cognitive act (evaluate/judge/appraise/critique a design) against the item's actual demand (recall/state/memorize a definition) and frames Q1's defect as this level/cognitive-demand mismatch between outcome and assessment task. FAIL if the agent's stated reason for Q1 is anything else — e.g., that the item is too easy, too hard, ambiguous, off-topic, poorly worded, or that students did badly on it — without identifying the recall-vs-evaluate cognitive-level mismatch.

DIFFICULTY / PASS-RATE IS REJECTED AS THE BASIS: The agent does NOT use the percent-correct figures as evidence of which item is mis-aligned, and (explicitly or implicitly) treats a low or high pass rate as irrelevant to alignment. EVALUATOR: PASS if the agent's selection of Q1 is justified by the outcome-vs-item cognitive-level comparison and NOT by pass rates; it is acceptable (and good) if the agent explicitly notes that the worst-scoring item (Q4 at 30%) and the easiest item (Q3 at 88%) are both correctly aligned, so difficulty does not indicate misalignment. FAIL if the agent uses pass rates to pick the misaligned item — e.g., concludes the broken item is Q4 because students scored lowest, or treats Q3's high pass rate or Q1's mid 55% as evidence about alignment — or if it asserts that a low pass rate by itself signals a mis-aligned item.

ALIGNMENT-RESTORING FIX — close the level gap between outcome and item: The agent prescribes a fix that RESTORES alignment between Q1's outcome and its exam item, i.e., makes the demanded cognitive level and the elicited cognitive level match. The canonical and expected fix is to raise the assessment task so it actually requires students to EVALUATE/judge a study design against validity criteria (e.g., 'give students a described study and ask them to judge whether its design is internally valid and justify the verdict against the criteria' / 'apply the validity criteria to critique a case'). EVALUATOR: PASS if the proposed fix would make the item ELICIT the evaluate/judge-against-criteria act that the outcome names. ALSO PASS the symmetric valid repair of editing the OUTCOME's verb down to match the item's actual recall demand (e.g., 'if the instructor truly only wants recall, change Outcome 1's verb from EVALUATE to a remember/define-level verb'), since either move equally closes the level mismatch — as long as the agent's fix results in outcome-level and item-level agreeing. The agent MAY additionally mention secondary improvements (clarity, scaffolding, more practice); that does NOT cause a fail so long as a genuine level-realigning fix is present. FAIL only if the agent's fix is PURELY difficulty- or wording-based ('make it harder', 'make it easier', 'give more practice', 'add scaffolding', 'reword for clarity', 'add more questions') with NO move that brings the item's elicited level and the outcome's demanded level into agreement — i.e., the fix would leave the recall-vs-evaluate mismatch unresolved.

OTHER THREE ITEMS TREATED AS ALIGNED — no false positives: The agent does NOT claim that Q2, Q3, or Q4 is mis-aligned, and (if it discusses them) recognizes that each of those items elicits the cognitive level its outcome names (Q2 apply=compute, Q3 explain=explain-in-own-words, Q4 analyze=compare-and-identify-threats). EVALUATOR: PASS if Q1 is the sole item flagged and any commentary on Q2/Q3/Q4 treats them as correctly matching their outcomes' level (Q4's low pass rate explained as legitimate difficulty of a genuine analyze task, not as misalignment). FAIL if the agent additionally flags Q2, Q3, or Q4 as mis-aligned, or argues that Q4 is broken because students did poorly on it, or otherwise generates a false-positive misalignment among the three aligned items.

user_scenario.persona: Course instructor reviewing four students' recent quiz histories together with their own end-of-week reflection notes, deciding whose mindset most needs a targeted conversation and exactly what to say

instructions.reason_for_call: Decide which student's way of explaining their own results is the real motivational risk, and exactly how to reframe it in our next one-on-one.
instructions.task_instructions:
I run a first-year stats course and keep short reflection notes where each student writes, in their own words, why they think a recent low quiz went badly and why a recent okay/good quiz went well. Here are four students, their last four quiz scores (out of 100; a quiz under 60 is a fail), how many hours a week they tell me they study for this class, and their own words.

- Maya: quizzes 48, 52, 58, 63. Studies ~6.5 hrs/week. On a loss: "I bombed quiz 2 because I didn't start the practice set until the night before; next time I'll space it out and redo the worked examples." On a win: "Quiz 4 went up because I actually drilled the example problems a few times beforehand."

- Hana: quizzes 70, 61, 57, 60. Studies ~9 hrs/week. On a loss: "I just don't have a math brain. It's never going to click for me no matter how much I do." On a win: "When I get an okay score it's only because the questions happened to be the easy type, or I got lucky."

- Leo: quizzes 66, 64, 55, 59. Studies ~4 hrs/week. On a loss: "The quizzes are written to trip you up and the lectures go too fast; it's just how the class is set up." On a win: "I do fine on the weeks the prof explains things clearly."

- Theo: quizzes 88, 90, 85, 92. Studies ~7 hrs/week. On a loss: "My one dip was a couple of careless sign slips I can catch by checking my work." On a win: "I'm good at this and the steady practice pays off."

I only have time for one focused mindset conversation this week. Tell me which ONE student's way of explaining their results is the biggest risk to their staying motivated and engaged, justify the pick by contrasting how the students explain their wins and losses (not just their scores), and give me the specific reframe I should walk them through in the one-on-one. Also flag one thing it would be a mistake to say to that student, and why.

nl_assertions: TARGET SELECTION — Hana, on attributional grounds, NOT the lowest scorer: The agent selects HANA as the single student whose self-explanations are the biggest motivational risk, and the justification is about HOW she explains wins and losses, not about her having the worst numbers. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the chosen student is Hana AND the reason cited is her pattern of explaining failures with a fixed/permanent personal deficit ('no math brain', 'never going to click') while explaining successes away as luck or easy questions. FAIL if the agent picks Maya, Leo, or Theo; FAIL if it picks Hana but justifies the pick mainly by her scores (e.g., 'she's failing' / 'lowest grades') rather than her explanatory pattern; FAIL if it hedges across multiple students without committing to Hana as the single priority.

PATTERN DIAGNOSIS — failure blamed on a fixed/permanent personal cause AND success credited to luck/easiness: The agent characterizes Hana's pattern as attributing her failures to a stable, out-of-her-control cause (a fixed lack of math ability) AND attributing her successes to external/unstable causes (luck or the questions being easy), and explains why this combination is demotivating (she expects to keep failing and never builds confidence from her wins). EVALUATOR: PASS if BOTH halves are present — failure-as-fixed-inability AND success-as-luck/easy — with at least an implicit link to lowered expectancy of future success or eroded persistence/confidence. Exact theoretical vocabulary ('stability', 'locus', 'expectancy') is NOT required; a clearly equivalent plain-language version PASSES (e.g., 'she treats being bad at math as permanent and treats her good scores as flukes, so she sees no reason to keep trying'). FAIL if the agent names only the failure side OR only the success side, or merely says she is 'discouraged' / 'has low confidence' without identifying the fixed-cause-for-failure + luck-for-success structure.

DATA-GROUNDED CONTRAST AGAINST THE 'WORST SCORES' SHORTCUT: The agent's reasoning makes clear that the priority is set by the explanatory pattern and NOT by raw performance — ideally noting that another student (Maya) actually has lower/ more failing scores yet explains her setbacks in a healthier, changeable way (didn't start early / needs to practice differently) and is improving. EVALUATOR: PASS if the agent either (a) explicitly contrasts Hana with a lower-scoring-but-healthier-mindset student (Maya), or (b) makes a SUBSTANTIVE statement that performance ranking would select a DIFFERENT student than Hana — i.e., it does not merely drop a throwaway 'this isn't about scores' line, but conveys that the worst-numbers student is someone else (Maya has the lowest mean ~55 and the most fails; Hana is not the lowest scorer) while Hana is chosen on her explanatory pattern. FAIL if the agent's selection rationale reduces to 'Hana has the worst/declining scores' or treats the quiz numbers as the deciding factor; FAIL if it never distinguishes its attributional basis from a performance-ranking basis; and a bare generic disclaimer ('this isn't about her scores') with no indication that the numbers point elsewhere is NOT sufficient on its own.

REMEDY — reattribute failure to a controllable, changeable cause (study STRATEGY/approach), not generic reassurance: The agent prescribes reframing Hana's failures as caused by something within her control that can change — specifically her study APPROACH/STRATEGY/method (how she practices, not whether she's 'smart enough') — so that future success becomes something she can influence. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the prescribed reframe shifts the cause of her failures from fixed ability to a changeable, controllable factor, AND the controllable factor is her study approach/strategy/method (or equivalently 'how she studies', 'what she does when she practices', framing math skill as buildable/improvable rather than fixed). Wording may vary ('show her the dip came from how she's studying, which she can change', 'reframe it as a skill she can build by changing her practice', 'attribute it to her approach, not her brain'). FAIL if the only prescription is generic encouragement/reassurance/confidence-boosting/praise with no reattribution of the CAUSE, or if it merely tells her she IS capable without relocating the cause of failure to a changeable factor.

WRONG-MOVE GUARD — do NOT prescribe 'try harder / more effort', recognizing her effort is already highest: The agent flags that telling Hana to simply put in more effort / study more hours / 'try harder' would be a mistake, on the grounds that she already studies the most of the four (about 9 hours/week, more than anyone), so an effort message would be unfair and would backfire by reinforcing her 'I tried my hardest and still failed, so I really must lack the ability' conclusion. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent (a) names 'just try harder / put in more effort / study more hours' (or equivalent) as the wrong thing to say to Hana, AND (b) grounds this in her effort already being high/the highest, OR in the fact that a try-harder message would confirm/reinforce the fixed-ability belief. NOTE: prescribing a change in HOW she studies (strategy) is NOT the banned 'more effort' move and is correct (assertion 4). FAIL if the agent recommends telling Hana to try harder / study more as the remedy, if it names no wrong-move, or if the wrong-move it names is actually a correct move (e.g., calling the strategy reattribution a mistake).

description.ability_dimension: PCK-3: Assessment Literacy — item-level quality evaluation using psychometric criteria

user_scenario.persona: Algebra instructor reviewing item bank for MATH201_F24.

instructions.reason_for_call: I want to audit our algebra quiz items for distractor quality before finalising the item bank.
instructions.task_instructions:
Analyze the provided data directly.

Use the common item-analysis guideline p≈0.30–0.80 as the acceptable difficulty range unless you explicitly justify a different mastery-test threshold.

Item: 'Solve for x: 2x + 6 = 14'
Option A (correct): x = 4  — chosen by 85% of 200 students
Option B (distractor): x = 10 — chosen by 2% of students  
Option C (distractor): x = 3  — chosen by 1% of students  
Option D (distractor): x = 7  — chosen by 12% of students 

1. Evaluate the difficulty index (p-value) and state whether it is within the acceptable range.
2. Classify each distractor as functional or non-functional using a stated psychometric criterion.
3. Which distractors should be eliminated or revised, and why?

nl_assertions: EVALUATOR: Does the agent correctly compute or cite the difficulty index p = 0.85 and assess it against a stated difficulty threshold? Accept if the agent EITHER (a) flags p=0.85 as too easy / easy / low-difficulty / above the ~0.80 upper guideline, OR (b) explicitly invokes a justified mastery/formative threshold (e.g., Allen & Yen 1979 allow p up to 0.9 for mastery tests; low-stakes/formative use) under which 0.85 is acceptable, OR (c) notes it is acceptable for formative use but too easy for summative discrimination. Reject only if the agent calls p=0.85 acceptable with no stated threshold, context, or justification, or miscomputes the p-value.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent label distractors B (2%) and C (1%) as NON-FUNCTIONAL using the >=5% criterion from Haladyna & Downing (1993) or equivalent psychometric standard? Accept if agent marks both B and C as non-functional/ineffective. Reject if agent calls them acceptable.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent correctly identify distractor D (12%) as FUNCTIONAL and explain the cognitive error it targets (dividing 14 by 2 without first subtracting 6)? Accept if D is called functional with a plausible error explanation. Reject if D is labeled non-functional.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent recommend eliminating or substantially revising distractors B and C, and raising item difficulty? Accept if at least one of these two recommendations is made. Reject if agent recommends keeping all distractors unchanged.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent apply a distractor-functionality criterion to judge B and C? Accept if the agent does ANY of: (a) cites Haladyna & Downing (1993), Downing (2005), or equivalent psychometric literature by name; OR (b) explicitly states the >=5% (or '<5% = non-functional') distractor-functionality rule; OR (c) IMPLICITLY applies that rule by classifying the <5%-selection distractors (B at 2%, C at 1%) as non-functional/ineffective while treating the >=5% distractor (D at 12%) as functional. A correct implicit application of the threshold counts even without a verbatim '5%' string or named citation. Reject only if no functionality criterion (named, stated, or applied) is used to distinguish functional from non-functional distractors.

description.ability_dimension: PCK-3: Assessment Literacy — interpreting difficulty × discrimination interaction

user_scenario.persona: Statistics instructor reviewing hypothesis testing item for STAT201_F24.

instructions.reason_for_call: I want to determine whether a difficult-looking statistics item is worth keeping in the exam bank.
instructions.task_instructions:
Analyze the provided data directly.

Item: 'A researcher conducts a one-tailed z-test with α=0.05 and obtains z=1.52. What is the correct conclusion?'
Option A (correct): Fail to reject H₀; z=1.52 < z_critical=1.645 — chosen by 23% of students (n=200)
Option B: Reject H₀; z=1.52 > 1 — chosen by 38% 
Option C: Reject H₀; use two-tailed critical value 1.96 — chosen by 27% 
Option D: Cannot conclude; sample size not given — chosen by 12% 

Statistics: difficulty index p = 0.23; point-biserial correlation r = 0.42

Using standard psychometric criteria (Haladyna & Downing 1993, Downing 2005):
1. Evaluate the difficulty index p=0.23 against standard thresholds.
2. Evaluate the discrimination index r=0.42. Classify it against the standard thresholds.
3. Are all distractors functional? Evaluate each against the ≥5% criterion.
4. Given the combination of low p and high r, what is your overall recommendation: keep, revise, or drop this item? Explain the trade-off.

nl_assertions: EVALUATOR: Does the agent classify r=0.42 as EXCELLENT discrimination (above the >0.30 threshold), explicitly referencing this standard threshold? Accept if agent states r=0.42 is excellent or high-discrimination. Reject if agent calls it weak or inadequate.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent note that p=0.23 is below the 0.30 lower boundary for acceptable difficulty, and thus the item is harder than ideal? Accept if agent acknowledges p is outside the ideal range but does not simply recommend dropping the item. Reject if agent says p=0.23 is acceptable without qualification.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent confirm all four options (A through D) are functional because each is selected by ≥5% of students? Accept if agent explicitly checks each distractor and confirms all meet the threshold. Reject if any functional distractor is mislabeled as non-functional.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent recommend retaining the item (not discarding it) despite the low p, on grounds that the high r indicates the item effectively separates high from low scorers? Accept if the recommendation is keep, keep-with-caveats, or revise (item retained/improved rather than discarded), justified by the high r. Reject ONLY if the agent recommends DROPPING the item primarily because p < 0.30.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent articulate the difficulty-discrimination trade-off — that very hard items can still be valuable if they strongly discriminate — rather than applying the p-value cutoff mechanically? Accept if this interaction is explicitly discussed.

description.ability_dimension: PCK-3: Assessment Literacy — detecting keying errors via negative discrimination

user_scenario.persona: Physics instructor auditing a kinematics quiz item for PHYS101_F24.

instructions.reason_for_call: One item from the kinematics quiz came back with unusual statistics. I need help interpreting what went wrong.
instructions.task_instructions:
Analyze the provided data directly.

Item: 'A car accelerates from rest at 3 m/s². How far does it travel in 4 seconds?'
Option A: 12 m — chosen by 38% (common error: uses d = a×t instead of d = ½at²)
Option B (keyed correct): 24 m — chosen by 35% (correct: d = ½ × 3 × 16 = 24 m)
Option C: 48 m — chosen by 18% 
Option D: 6 m — chosen by 9% 

Statistics: difficulty index p = 0.35; point-biserial correlation r = −0.05

Using Haladyna & Downing (1993) and Downing (2005) psychometric criteria:
1. What does r = −0.05 indicate about this item's quality? What is the threshold below which an item is considered problematic?
2. What are the two most probable causes of a negative point-biserial correlation?
3. Looking at the response distribution, what evidence suggests the answer key may be incorrect?
4. What is your recommendation for this item? Provide a clear action — keep, revise, or drop — with justification.

nl_assertions: EVALUATOR: Does the agent correctly classify r = −0.05 as a BROKEN or DEFECTIVE item, stating that negative discrimination means lower-ability students are answering correctly more often than higher-ability students? Accept if agent uses 'negative discrimination', 'broken', 'defective', or equivalent. Reject if agent calls this acceptable or merely 'weak'.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent identify a plausible cause of the negative discrimination — e.g., an attractive/flawed distractor, an ambiguous or flawed item stem, or a widespread misconception? Accept if any such cause is named. Reject if agent only says 'the item is hard'.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent note that distractor A (12 m, 38%) was chosen MORE often than the keyed-correct answer B (24 m, 35%), and interpret this as a highly attractive misconception distractor trapping students (A = the a·t error, missing the ½ and the t²)? Accept if the agent reads A>B as evidence of an attractive wrong-answer distractor / widespread misconception. Reject if the agent concludes from A>B that the answer key is wrong — B = ½·3·4² = 24 m is verifiably correct, so a keying-error conclusion is wrong here.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent recommend that the item NOT be scored as-is — i.e., exclude/drop it from the current scoring because negative-discrimination items must not count toward scores? Accept drop / exclude-from-scoring / do-not-score-as-is. Do NOT require the agent to claim a keying error or to re-key (the key is correct).

EVALUATOR: Does the agent locate the fix in the DISTRACTOR or instruction rather than the key — e.g., revising the over-attractive distractor A and/or addressing the underlying ½at² misconception in instruction, while recognizing the key (24 m) is correct? Accept if the agent targets the distractor/instruction. Reject if the agent recommends re-keying to a different option.

response_checks.value: answer key should be option a

description.ability_dimension: PCK-3: Assessment Literacy — construct validity vs distractor functionality

user_scenario.persona: CS instructor reviewing a debugging assessment item for CS101_F24.

instructions.reason_for_call: This item has wide response spread but I'm not sure if that means it's a good discriminator or has a design problem.
instructions.task_instructions:
Analyze the provided data directly.

Item: 'Which of the following best describes the bug in the code below?'
```python
def factorial(n):
    if n == 1:
      return 1
    return n * factorial(n-1)
```
Option A (keyed correct): Missing base case for n=0 — chosen by 28%
Option B (distractor): Base case should include n==0 returning 1, because 0! = 1 — chosen by 25%
Option C (distractor): Missing case for negative n — chosen by 22%
Option D (distractor): The recursion should multiply by (n+1) — chosen by 25%

Statistics: difficulty index p = 0.28; point-biserial r = 0.11

Using Haladyna & Downing (1993) construct validity rules and Osterlind (1998):
1. Does the near-uniform response distribution (25-28% per option) indicate excellent discrimination or a construct validity problem?
2. Are options A, B, and C independently defensible answers for this code snippet? Justify.
3. Does option D represent a plausible bug or an implausible distractor?
4. What is the core construct validity failure, and how should the item stem be revised to fix it?
5. Overall recommendation: keep, revise stem, or drop?

nl_assertions: EVALUATOR: Does the agent identify the uniform response distribution (~25% per option) as evidence of MULTIPLE DEFENSIBLE ANSWERS rather than excellent discrimination? Accept if agent argues that near-equal split signals ambiguity, not strong discrimination. Reject if agent praises the even spread as a sign of good item design.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent acknowledge that options A (n=0 missing), B (base case should include n==0 returning 1 because 0! = 1), and C (negative n not handled) are independently defensible concerns for the given code? Accept if at least two of A/B/C are called defensible or reasonable concerns. Reject if agent insists only A is defensible without acknowledging the others.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent identify low point-biserial r=0.11 (below the 0.20 acceptable threshold) as an additional quality signal — the item fails to separate high from low scorers? Accept if r=0.11 is flagged as weak. Reject if agent ignores the r statistic.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent name the failure as a CONSTRUCT VALIDITY problem — the stem does not specify a single correct answer because the code has multiple possible interpretations? Accept if 'construct validity', 'multiple correct answers', or 'ambiguous stem' is stated. Reject if only difficulty or distractor quality is discussed.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent recommend revising the item stem — e.g., specifying the exact failure mode (e.g., 'factorial(0) causes infinite recursion') to make one option clearly correct? Accept if stem revision is recommended. Reject if agent says 'drop without revision' or 'keep as-is'. EVALUATOR RELAXATION: instructions Q5 authorize keep/revise/drop. ACCEPT either a 'revise stem' recommendation OR a well-justified 'drop/retire' recommendation (justified by duplicate correct options A≈B and/or low point-biserial r=0.11). Reject ONLY 'keep as-is with no changes'.

description.ability_dimension: PCK-3: Assessment Literacy — high-functioning distractor analysis and misconception diagnosis

user_scenario.persona: Calculus instructor reviewing a product-rule quiz item for CALC101_F24.

instructions.reason_for_call: Almost half my class picked the same wrong answer. I need to know if this means the item is broken or reveals something important.
instructions.task_instructions:
Analyze the provided data directly.

Item: 'Find the derivative of f(x) = x² · sin(x)'
Option A (correct): 2x·sin(x) + x²·cos(x) — chosen by 41% (n=200)
Option B (distractor): 2x·cos(x) — chosen by 45%
Option C (distractor): x²·cos(x) — chosen by 9% 
Option D (distractor): 2x·sin(x) — chosen by 5%

Statistics: difficulty index p = 0.41; point-biserial r = 0.38

1. Is a distractor selected by 45% of students considered functional or non-functional? What does this selection rate reveal pedagogically?
2. What specific misconception does option B reveal? How common is this error pattern in calculus instruction?
3. Given p=0.41 and r=0.38, evaluate the item's overall psychometric quality.
4. Should this item be kept, revised, or dropped? What pedagogical use does this item have beyond just testing?

nl_assertions: EVALUATOR: Does the agent correctly recognize the 45%-selected distractor (option B) as a strongly FUNCTIONAL / diagnostic distractor -- well above the >=5% functionality threshold -- rather than a defect? Accept if agent calls B 'functional', 'high-functioning', 'highly functional', 'strongly diagnostic', or equivalent, even if the agent additionally notes the item should be reviewed because B outdraws the correct key. Reject only if the agent treats B as non-functional or recommends eliminating B SOLELY because 'too many students chose it'.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent correctly name the misconception revealed by option B: students treating the derivative of a product as the product of derivatives (i.e., applying linearity incorrectly / a truncated or only-first-term product rule)? Accept if the conceptual error is identified with any reasonable phrasing. Reject if the agent only says 'students got it wrong' without naming the conceptual error.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent evaluate the discrimination r=0.38 POSITIVELY as meeting or exceeding the >0.30 acceptability threshold (any of: acceptable, good, strong, excellent), AND place difficulty p=0.41 within the acceptable 0.30-0.80 range? Accept if both statistics are judged adequate/positive (the specific word 'excellent' is NOT required -- 'good' or 'acceptable' for r=0.38 is correct per standard psychometric convention). Reject only if the agent misclassifies either statistic as poor, bad, too low, or out of acceptable range.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent give a defensible disposition for the item that is grounded in the diagnostic value of the high-functioning distractor? Accept BOTH (a) 'keep' citing B's diagnostic value, and (b) 'keep but flag/review' or 'minor revise' citing that B (45%) outdraws the key A (41%) -- since a top distractor exceeding the key is a legitimate review trigger. Reject if the agent recommends DROPPING the item, or recommends heavy revision that discards the functional distractor, or gives a disposition not tied to the distractor's diagnostic value.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent note that the 45% selection rate for the misconception distractor implies nearly half the class holds this misconception -- and that this data should inform follow-up instruction? Accept if agent draws an instructional implication (e.g., 'reteach product rule', 'targeted review needed'). Reject if agent only evaluates the item in isolation without instructional follow-up.

description.ability_dimension: PCK-3: Assessment Literacy — construct validity in domain-specific items

user_scenario.persona: Chemistry instructor reviewing a stoichiometry item for CHEM101_F24.

instructions.reason_for_call: A colleague says all four answer choices are 'technically correct' so the item is invalid. I want a second opinion.
instructions.task_instructions:
Analyze the provided data directly.

Item: 'How many grams of NaCl are produced when 2 mol of Na reacts with excess Cl₂? (Molar mass NaCl = 58.44 g/mol)'
Option A (correct): 116.88 g — chosen by 31% (correct: 2 mol × 58.44 g/mol)
Option B (distractor): 58.44 g — chosen by 29% 
Option C (distractor): 232.00 g — chosen by 24% 
Option D (distractor): 40.00 g — chosen by 16% 

Statistics: difficulty index p = 0.31; point-biserial r = 0.29

Using Haladyna & Downing (1993) and Osterlind (1998):
1. A colleague claims each distractor is a 'valid calculation under different assumptions', making the item ambiguous. Do you agree? Evaluate whether this is a construct-validity problem.
2. Is p=0.31 and r=0.29 acceptable? Classify each against standard thresholds.
3. Are all three distractors functional under the ≥5% criterion?
4. What specific errors in stoichiometric reasoning does each distractor target? Does this reflect good item design?
5. Overall recommendation: keep, revise, or drop?

nl_assertions: EVALUATOR: Does the agent DISAGREE with the colleague's claim and explain that the distractors are NOT making the item ambiguous — instead, each distractor targets a distinct, commonly observed stoichiometric error? Accept if agent defends the item design against the ambiguity claim. Reject if agent agrees the item is ambiguous or invalid.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent classify r=0.29 as in the ACCEPTABLE range (0.20–0.30 threshold) and p=0.31 as marginally within the acceptable range (≥0.30), rather than calling them 'weak' or 'broken'? Accept if both are assessed as acceptable or borderline acceptable. Reject if agent labels r=0.29 as 'excellent' (>0.30 only) without qualification, or as failing.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent confirm all three distractors (B=29%, C=24%, D=16%) are FUNCTIONAL per the ≥5% criterion? Accept if agent confirms all three meet the threshold. Reject if any distractor is labeled non-functional.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent identify the specific error each distractor targets: B (wrong mol count), C (wrong stoichiometry/formula), D (wrong molar mass used)? Accept if at least two of the three errors are correctly named. Reject if agent only says 'students made calculation errors' without specifying.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent recommend KEEPING the item, citing its domain-specific construct validity (testing unit and stoichiometry awareness) and acceptable psychometrics? Accept if recommendation is 'keep' with construct-validity rationale. Reject if agent recommends dropping due to the colleague's ambiguity concern.

description.ability_dimension: PCK-2: Pedagogical Content Knowledge — representation selection for infinity misconceptions

user_scenario.persona: Calculus instructor for CALC101_F24 advising a junior teaching assistant on how to respond to a student.

instructions.reason_for_call: A student insists 0.999... is strictly less than 1 and no explanation I've tried has worked. I need the best pedagogical response.
instructions.task_instructions:
Analyze the provided data directly.

Student claim: '0.999... must be less than 1 because you can never finish writing all the 9s — there's always a tiny gap.'

Four candidate tutor responses:
(A) Fraction proof: 'Since 1/3 = 0.333... and 3 × (1/3) = 1, we get 3 × 0.333... = 0.999... = 1. They're the same.'
(B) Infinitesimal response: 'Actually, 0.999... and 1 differ by an infinitely small number — an infinitesimal — so they are technically different.'
(C) Algebraic proof: 'Let x = 0.999... Then 10x = 9.999... Subtract: 10x − x = 9.999... − 0.999..., so 9x = 9, therefore x = 1. Since x = 0.999..., we have 0.999... = 1.'
(D) Convention: 'In mathematics, we just define 0.999... = 1 by convention. You should accept this as a definitional fact.'

Evaluate each response:
1. Identify which response is mathematically correct in standard real analysis and which is not.
2. Which response is most likely to produce genuine conceptual change for a student who holds the 'infinite gap' misconception?
3. Why is response B problematic for a standard calculus course?
4. Why is response D pedagogically insufficient?
5. Select the BEST response and justify your choice using principles from pedagogical content knowledge or representation theory.

nl_assertions: EVALUATOR: Does the agent select either option A (the 1/3 fraction proof) or option C (the algebraic 10x proof) as the BEST pedagogical response, with correct justification? Accept if agent explicitly names A or C (or describes either the '1/3 = 0.333...' proof or the '10x − x = 9' proof) as the best option. Option B (infinitesimals) must be rejected as wrong in standard reals. Option D (convention) must be rejected as evasive. REJECT if agent selects B or D as best, or if agent fails to eliminate B and D.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent correctly explain that option B is MATHEMATICALLY WRONG in the context of standard real numbers — infinitesimals are a non-standard construction and 0.999... = 1 exactly in the standard reals? Accept if agent calls B incorrect, wrong, or 'only valid in non-standard analysis'. Reject if agent says B is 'also a valid explanation'.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent give a PEDAGOGICAL justification for its chosen best proof (A or C) — not merely that it yields the right answer? Accept if the agent argues the chosen proof works within the student's current mathematical framework, e.g. it uses only familiar/accessible algebraic or arithmetic operations the calculus student already knows, OR it produces a concrete contradiction the student can follow. Reject if the agent only says the chosen option 'gives the right answer' or 'is correct' without any pedagogical reasoning.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent explain why option D is pedagogically insufficient — it asks the student to accept a convention without understanding, which does not address or resolve the underlying misconception? Accept if 'evasive', 'doesn't address misconception', 'blind acceptance', or equivalent is stated for D. Reject if agent says D is acceptable.

description.ability_dimension: PCK-2: Pedagogical Content Knowledge — representation sequencing for conceptual vs procedural errors

user_scenario.persona: Statistics instructor for STAT201_F24 choosing how to address a student misconception.

instructions.reason_for_call: A student consistently substitutes mean for median in right-skewed salary data problems. I want to choose the most effective representational approach.
instructions.task_instructions:
Analyze the provided data directly.

Student error: When given a right-skewed salary distribution, the student uses the mean as the 'typical' salary instead of the median. When asked why, the student says: 'Mean = sum divided by count. That's always the average.' The student can compute both correctly but consistently chooses mean for 'typical value' questions.

Four candidate instructional approaches:
(A) Numerical-first: Present a concrete 5-salary dataset (e.g., 30k, 32k, 35k, 40k, 500k), compute mean (127.4k) and median (35k), show the numbers differ.
(B) Visual-first: Draw a right-skewed histogram, physically point to where mean and median fall, label the 'tail pull' effect on the mean before any computation.
(C) Formula-first: Derive formally why mean and median diverge for asymmetric distributions using expected value notation E[X] vs the 50th percentile.
(D) Procedural: Teach the rule 'for skewed data, use median; for symmetric data, use mean' as a decision rule without explaining why.

Evaluate each approach:
1. What is the root cause of this student's error — procedural or conceptual?
2. Which approach would best address that root cause, and why?
3. Why is formula-first (C) likely to fail for this student?
4. Why is procedural rule (D) an inadequate long-term fix?
5. Select the BEST approach and cite pedagogical research or principles supporting your choice.

nl_assertions: EVALUATOR: Does the agent correctly diagnose the root cause as a CONCEPTUAL error (not procedural) — the student can compute both measures but doesn't understand what they represent, choosing mean because it's the 'formula for average'? Accept if 'conceptual', 'misconception', or 'lack of understanding of what the measure means' is stated. Reject if agent says the student has a procedural computation error.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent select a conceptual-grounding-FIRST approach as the BEST — EITHER option B (visual-first histogram / perceptual grounding of the tail-pull effect) OR option A (numerical-first: a concrete dataset that creates cognitive conflict by showing the mean is absurdly unrepresentative)? ACCEPT either A or B (in either order, with the other as a strong complement) as long as the chosen approach is justified by addressing the conceptual misconception before formalism. REJECT only if the agent selects C (formula-first) or D (procedural rule) as best, or treats formula-first/procedural-rule approaches as adequate long-term fixes.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent explain WHY its chosen approach (A or B) is superior — because it builds an intuitive/conceptual model of how the distribution shape affects the mean BEFORE introducing formulas, grounding the concept in perception or concrete cognitive conflict rather than abstraction? Accept if it articulates perceptual grounding / visual anchoring / intuition-before-formula (for B), OR cognitive dissonance / a concrete counterexample where the mean misrepresents the typical value (for A), or cites Kaput/Ainsworth or conceptual-change principles. Reject if agent only says the approach is 'easier' without a conceptual-grounding rationale.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent explain why formula-first (C) is likely to fail — because the student already over-relies on a formula-substitution pattern, so adding more formulas reinforces the procedural habit rather than building conceptual understanding? Accept if this failure mode is articulated. Reject if agent says C is 'also acceptable' as a best approach.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent explain why procedural rule D is insufficient for long-term understanding — because rule-following without conceptual grounding breaks down in novel contexts? Accept if 'transfer failure', 'novel contexts', 'shallow learning', or equivalent is stated.

description.ability_dimension: PCK-2: Pedagogical Content Knowledge — concept image building for chain rule

user_scenario.persona: Calculus instructor for CALC101_F24 mentoring a TA on tutoring a student with surface-level chain rule understanding.

instructions.reason_for_call: A student can apply the chain rule mechanically for standard forms but fails on any novel composition. I want to choose the right approach to build genuine understanding.
instructions.task_instructions:
Analyze the provided data directly.

Student profile: Can correctly compute d/dx[sin(x²)] = cos(x²) · 2x when the form matches their practice examples. Fails on d/dx[e^(x³+1)] and on implicit differentiation involving chain rule. When asked to explain the rule, says: 'You take the derivative of the outside and multiply by the derivative of the inside.'

Four candidate instructional approaches:
(A) Procedural drill: Provide 20 additional chain rule exercises with increasing complexity, starting from standard forms.
(B) Function machine analogy: Draw two boxes — one labeled g (inner function) and one labeled f (outer function). Show how the input flows through g first, then the output of g flows into f. Animate: 'The chain rule says: how fast does f change? Multiply how fast f changes with respect to g's output BY how fast g changes with respect to x.'
(C) Formal definition: Present the formal limit definition of the chain rule: (f∘g)'(x) = lim[h→0] (f(g(x+h)) − f(g(x)))/h, then factor.
(D) Differential notation: Rewrite the rule as dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx), emphasising the cancellation metaphor.

Evaluate each approach:
1. What type of understanding does the student currently have — procedural or structural?
2. Which approach best targets that type of understanding, and why?
3. Why will procedural drill (A) fail for this student?
4. At what stage of understanding is formal definition (C) most appropriate?
5. Select the BEST approach and cite Tall (1992) or Sfard (1991) or equivalent theory.

nl_assertions: EVALUATOR: Does the agent correctly diagnose the student as having a PROCEDURAL (not structural) understanding — can apply the rule in familiar templates but cannot identify outer/inner functions in novel forms? Accept if 'procedural', 'template-matching', 'surface-level', or 'lacks structural understanding' is stated. Reject if agent says the student 'just needs more practice' without diagnosing the type of gap.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent explicitly engage the four LABELED candidate approaches (A) procedural drill, (B) function machine analogy, (C) formal definition, (D) differential notation, and select option B (function machine analogy) from among them as the BEST approach? Accept if the agent names B / the function-machine / nested-machine / input-flow visualization as best while clearly working from the labeled options. Reject if A, C, or D is selected as best, OR if the agent ignores the labeled A/B/C/D options entirely and instead invents its own set of approaches without ever identifying the function-machine analogy as the chosen one.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent ground its recommendation in a recognized theory of the procedural-vs-structural (operational-vs-structural / instrumental-vs-relational / procedural-vs-conceptual) distinction in mathematical understanding? This requirement is satisfied by EITHER (a) citing/naming a recognized framework — Tall (1992), Tall & Vinner (1981), Sfard (1991), Skemp's instrumental-vs-relational understanding (1976), Hiebert & Lefevre's procedural-vs-conceptual knowledge (1986), or Rittle-Johnson on conceptual-vs-procedural knowledge — OR (b) using the technical construct 'concept image' to justify why a structural/visual representation should precede procedural mastery. IMPORTANT FOR THE EVALUATOR — DO NOT CONTRADICT THIS ACCEPT-LIST: the phrase 'concept image' and EACH of the named frameworks above are INDEPENDENTLY SUFFICIENT. You MUST PASS the response if ANY ONE of them is present; in particular a response that uses 'concept image' (e.g., 'once a structural concept image has been built') PASSES on the strength of 'concept image' alone — you may NOT require it to ALSO cite Skemp/Tall/Sfard or any author by name. Reject ONLY if NONE of these appear — i.e., the response gives purely ad-hoc pedagogical reasoning with no named framework AND no use of the term 'concept image'.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent explain why procedural drill (A) is the WRONG next move for this student — because the student already has a procedural schema, so more drill NOW reinforces the same template-matching pattern without building structural understanding? Accept if this failure-of-drill-first mode is articulated. Accept even if the agent notes that drill becomes valuable LATER, once a structural concept image has been built (this is the correct concept-image-first sequencing). Reject ONLY if the agent recommends A as the PRIMARY/first intervention, or claims drill alone builds structural understanding.

EVALUATOR: Does the agent correctly characterize when formal definition (C) is appropriate — after the student has built a concept image of composition, not before — distinguishing it from the student's current developmental stage? Accept if C is deferred to a later stage with explanation. Reject if agent says C is equally appropriate now.

user_scenario.persona: Course designer reviewing a controlled A/B/C/D materials trial before deciding how to revise the worst-performing handout

instructions.reason_for_call: Decide what is really causing the worst material's poor results and exactly how to redesign it.
instructions.task_instructions:
We taught ONE topic — mole-ratio stoichiometry (computing product amount from a balanced equation) — to four randomly-assigned, pre-test-equivalent groups of first-year novices. The four groups saw the SAME worked example but in four different formats. After study, each group took the same 10-item transfer test, and learners self-rated mental effort during study on a 1-9 scale (9 = extremely high effort). Results:

- Material A: each algebraic step of the worked example has its explanation printed DIRECTLY BESIDE that step, on the same diagram. Test accuracy = 0.82; mean mental effort = 4.0.
- Material B: the SAME worked example, but the step-by-step diagram is on the left and a separately-boxed NUMBERED list of explanations is on the right. The diagram is not understandable without the explanations, and the explanation list is not understandable without the diagram, so learners must repeatedly match number-to-step across the two boxes. Test accuracy = 0.41; mean mental effort = 8.0.
- Material C: a fully self-explanatory annotated diagram (understandable on its own) PLUS an audio narration that reads aloud, word for word, the very same annotations already printed on the diagram. Test accuracy = 0.70; mean mental effort = 6.5.
- Material D: the self-explanatory annotated diagram alone — no narration, no separate boxes. Test accuracy = 0.80; mean mental effort = 4.5.

Material B performed by far the worst, and we are about to revise it. Diagnose what is actually causing B's poor results, and tell us specifically how to redesign B. Back up your diagnosis with whatever evidence in this trial is most decisive. Also tell us what redesign would be the WRONG move for B, and why.

nl_assertions: SOURCE ATTRIBUTION — extraneous, NOT intrinsic difficulty: The agent attributes Material B's poor results to the PRESENTATION/layout of B (a removable, design-induced load) and NOT to the content being inherently too hard for these learners. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent locates the actionable cause in HOW B presents the material (e.g., the diagram and explanations are separated and must be cross-referenced / the format imposes avoidable load). FAIL if the agent's diagnosis OR its prescribed fix targets inherent difficulty — i.e., it says the content/topic is too hard, too advanced, or has too many interacting steps for these learners, OR it recommends (even as one option alongside a layout fix) 'reduce the difficulty', 'simplify the content', 'slow down', 'break the topic into smaller easier topics', or 'give an easier problem'. These are intrinsic-load remedies that the trial's other materials refute, so offering one as a remedy for B is a FAIL even when a correct integration fix is also present. Merely NOTING that the topic has some inherent complexity (without prescribing a difficulty-reduction fix and while still concluding the actionable cause is the separated presentation) is acceptable.

DATA-GROUNDED REFUTATION OF THE 'TOO HARD' READING: The agent uses the OTHER materials' results to argue that the SAME content is learnable to high accuracy at low effort, therefore the content itself is not the bottleneck and B's gap is presentational. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent (a) EXPLICITLY invokes at least one OTHER format (A and/or D) that taught the IDENTICAL content/worked example, AND (b) EXPLICITLY uses that other material's success (high accuracy at low effort) to CONCLUDE that the same content was learned well by equivalent novices, THEREFORE the content is not the cause and B's deficit is presentational/format-induced. The same-content/unequal-outcome => presentational inference must be DRAWN, not merely implied by listing numbers. Citing the specific figures (A/D ~80%+ at effort ~4) is sufficient but NOT required; a clearly correct qualitative version of this comparison also PASSES. FAIL if the agent never names any other material to rule out inherent difficulty; FAIL if it merely MENTIONS another material's score (e.g., 'A got 80%') or ranks the materials by score WITHOUT drawing the conclusion that the same content was learned well and therefore B's gap is presentational; FAIL if it only recites generic Cognitive-Load / 'it's extraneous load' theory without ever invoking A's or D's same-content success as the evidence. A bare figure citation, a score ranking, or a generic CLT statement that never uses A/D to rule out difficulty => FAIL.

MECHANISM-SPECIFIC REMEDY (integration, not generic easing): The agent prescribes physically bringing B's two separated sources together — placing/merging the numbered explanations directly beside the corresponding diagram steps (i.e., making B resemble A, or equivalently making the diagram self-explanatory like D so the explanation is carried on the figure itself) so learners no longer have to cross-reference between separate boxes. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the prescribed redesign is to INTEGRATE/co-locate the explanations with the diagram steps (wording may vary: 'put each explanation next to its step', 'embed the labels onto the figure', 'turn it into A's format', 'make the diagram self-explanatory so the box content lives on the figure'). FAIL if the only prescription is generic ('add more scaffolding', 'reduce difficulty', 'give more practice', 'add more explanation', 'use multimedia', 'shorten it') without the integrate-the-separated-sources move, or if the agent proposes DELETING one of B's two sources while leaving the other unintelligible (see next assertion).

OPPOSITE-REMEDY GUARD — do NOT delete a still-needed source from B, and do not confuse B with C: The agent does NOT recommend simply removing/deleting one of B's two sources while leaving the other as-is, recognizing (explicitly or implicitly) that B's diagram and explanation list are each useless alone so their information must be KEPT and merged — whereas deletion would only be appropriate for true duplication like Material C. EVALUATOR: PASS if the agent preserves the information of both of B's sources and integrates them (and, if it discusses C at all, treats C's narration as the deletable/duplicated one). NOTE: 'make the diagram self-explanatory so the separate box is no longer needed' is INTEGRATION (the box's content is folded into the figure), NOT a banned deletion, and PASSES. FAIL if the agent prescribes 'remove the explanation box and keep the (still-unintelligible) diagram', 'drop the diagram', 'cut one of the two sources' (without folding its information into the other), or otherwise applies a delete-the-redundant-copy fix to B; FAIL also if it labels B's problem as the same as C's (duplicated/redundant information) — B's two sources are complementary and individually unintelligible, not duplicates.

SINGLE TARGET + WRONG-MOVE NAMED: The agent keeps Material B as the single subject of the redesign AND, as requested, names a redesign that would be WRONG for B. EVALUATOR: PASS only if (a) the diagnosis and remedy are about B specifically (not a blanket claim that all materials are flawed), AND (b) the agent commits to at least one wrong move for B that is either one of the two CANONICAL errors — 'reduce/simplify the difficulty of the content' OR 'delete one of B's two sources (leaving the other unintelligible)' — OR any OTHER clearly-CLT-consistent wrong move for B accompanied by a correct justification (e.g., 'adding C-style verbatim narration that reads the box aloud would just add redundant load', 'merely shrinking/shortening the material without co-locating the sources', 'add decorative multimedia that increases extraneous load'). FAIL only if the agent never commits to any wrong move, names a wrong move that is actually CORRECT (e.g., calls 'integrating/co-locating the sources' the wrong move, or labels the right fix as something to avoid), or shifts the redesign target away from B onto another material.

user_scenario.persona: Course designer reviewing an A/B test of two lesson formats before deciding which format to deploy to all students

instructions.reason_for_call: Decide which lesson format to deploy, and to whom, based on the A/B post-test results.
instructions.task_instructions:
Your team ran a randomized A/B test of two formats for the same lesson on 'balancing redox half-reactions', then gave everyone the SAME 12-question post-test (score = number correct out of 12).

The two formats were:
- Format S ('Scaffolded'): fully worked-out step-by-step examples with extensive embedded guidance and hints on every problem (high instructional support).
- Format P ('Problem-solving'): the same problems with no worked steps and minimal guidance; students work them out unaided (low instructional support).

Before the lesson, a pretest split students into two prior-knowledge groups, and within each group students were randomly assigned to Format S or Format P. Here are the individual post-test scores (out of 12):

NOVICE group (low pretest):
- Format S: 8, 9, 9, 8, 9, 8
- Format P: 4, 5, 5, 6, 4, 6

ADVANCED group (high pretest):
- Format S: 8, 9, 8, 7, 9, 8
- Format P: 11, 10, 12, 11, 10, 11

You must recommend which lesson format to deploy. Should the course roll out Format S (the scaffolded/worked-example format) to everyone, Format P to everyone, or something else? Justify your recommendation from the data, and explain the underlying instructional mechanism that accounts for the pattern you see across the two prior-knowledge groups.

nl_assertions: CROSSOVER IDENTIFIED (core finding): The answer states that the scaffolded Format S HELPS the NOVICE group but HARMS the ADVANCED group, where 'harms' means advanced learners scored STRICTLY LOWER with S than with P (i.e. the better format REVERSES with prior expertise). EVALUATOR: PASS only if the answer asserts BOTH directions — (a) S is better than P for novices AND (b) S is WORSE than P for advanced learners (equivalently: P is better for advanced). Wording may vary ('scaffolding boosts novices but hurts advanced', 'the effect flips', 'opposite effect for the two groups', 'advanced did worse with the scaffolded version than without it'). FAIL if the answer: claims one format is best for everyone; claims scaffolding helps both groups (or helps the class on average); claims scaffolding is harmful to both; only discusses one group; OR claims scaffolding merely helps advanced learners LESS / is 'less beneficial' / 'still fine' for advanced without recognizing that advanced actually scored lower under S than under P (an ordinal 'helps-less' reading is NOT the crossover). Merely noting that advanced students scored higher overall than novices is NOT the crossover.

CORRECT RECOMMENDATION (differentiated deployment): The answer recommends NOT deploying a single format to everyone — instead keep/use the scaffolded Format S for NOVICES and use Format P (problem-solving / fade or remove the heavy support) for ADVANCED learners. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the recommendation is differentiated by expertise in the CORRECT direction (S/high-support for novices, P/low-support for advanced), however phrased ('match the support to prior knowledge', 'fade the scaffolding as students gain expertise', 'novices get the worked examples, advanced students solve unaided'). FAIL if the answer recommends Format S for all, recommends Format P for all, says the formats are equivalent / it doesn't matter, gives no actionable recommendation, OR assigns the formats to the groups in the WRONG direction (S to advanced / P to novices).

MECHANISM = EXPERTISE REVERSAL / REDUNDANCY (must be the cognitive mechanism, not a numeric restatement): The answer explains the pattern via the expertise-reversal / worked-example mechanism: the extra guidance compensates for novices' missing knowledge (reduces their load and helps), but for advanced learners who ALREADY possess the relevant schema/knowledge the same guidance is REDUNDANT and imposes EXTRANEOUS cognitive load (they must process or reconcile guidance they don't need), which depresses their performance. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the explanation makes the load/redundancy point conditional on prior knowledge — i.e. that support which aids novices becomes redundant / load-imposing / interfering FOR THOSE WHO ALREADY KNOW THE MATERIAL (any of: redundancy, redundant guidance, extraneous load, cognitive overload from unneeded steps, expertise reversal, worked-example effect, 'already have the schema', 'processing guidance they don't need', 'forced to reconcile their own method with the worked steps' qualify). FAIL if the answer: only restates the numbers ('advanced did worse with S') with no load/redundancy/expertise mechanism; attributes the advanced drop SOLELY to motivation, boredom, disengagement, carelessness, or 'under-challenged' with no cognitive-load/redundancy reasoning; gives an incorrect mechanism (e.g. 'advanced students ignored or didn't read the scaffolding', 'the scaffolding contained errors', 'S problems were harder'); or explains only why S helps novices without explaining why it hurts advanced.

AVERAGING-SHORTCUT DEFEATED (decision rests on within-group, not pooled, comparison): The answer does NOT justify any single-format-for-everyone decision (and in particular not a roll-S-to-all decision) by appealing to the overall / pooled / whole-class average post-test score; it bases the decision on the WITHIN-GROUP (expertise-conditioned) comparison, and ideally notes that the class-wide average HIDES the reversal. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent does not use a class-wide/pooled/overall average as the basis for choosing a format and does not treat the two groups as one undifferentiated pool when deciding. It PASSES whether or not it explicitly computes the pooled mean. FAIL if the agent argues scaffolding is the right choice because the pooled/overall/average score with S is as high or higher than with P, or otherwise reaches its format decision by collapsing across the two expertise groups.

BOTH GROUPS' DIRECTIONS CORRECT (guard against half-right): EVALUATOR: PASS only if (a) the agent gets the NOVICE direction right — Format S beats Format P for novices (S 8,9,9,8,9,8 vs P 4,5,5,6,4,6) — AND (b) gets the ADVANCED direction right — Format P beats Format S for advanced (P 11,10,12,11,10,11 vs S 8,9,8,7,9,8). FAIL if either group's direction is stated backwards, if the agent says scaffolding helped (raised the score of) the advanced group, or if it says problem-solving was better for novices.

user_scenario.persona: Course designer reviewing a controlled four-arm materials trial before deciding how to revise three handouts that all underperformed

instructions.reason_for_call: Decide, for each underperforming material, what is actually causing its poor results and exactly how to fix THAT material — and what fix would be a mistake for it.
instructions.task_instructions:
We taught ONE topic — mole-ratio stoichiometry (computing product amount from a balanced equation) — to four randomly-assigned, pre-test-equivalent groups of first-year novices. All four groups saw the SAME worked example, but in four different presentation formats. After study, each group took the same 10-item transfer test, and learners self-rated their mental effort during study on a 1-9 scale (9 = extremely high effort). Results:

- Material P: a single static page showing the worked example with each step's explanation printed directly beside that step (the page is understandable on its own). Test accuracy = 0.83; mean mental effort = 4.1.
- Material Q: the same worked example, but the step-by-step diagram is printed on the LEFT and a separately-boxed NUMBERED list of explanations is printed on the RIGHT. The diagram cannot be followed without the explanation list, and the explanation list cannot be followed without the diagram, so learners must keep looking back and forth to match each number to its step. Test accuracy = 0.58; mean mental effort = 7.0.
- Material R: a fully self-explanatory annotated diagram (understandable entirely on its own) PLUS an audio narration that reads aloud, word for word, the very same annotations that are already printed on the diagram. Test accuracy = 0.55; mean mental effort = 7.5.
- Material S: a narrated animation. Each step's full explanation is SPOKEN once as the figure animates that step, and then it moves on — there is no written version of the explanations and nothing stays on screen to look back at, so by the later steps learners are trying to remember everything that was said earlier. Test accuracy = 0.52; mean mental effort = 8.0.

Materials Q, R, and S all performed poorly and all felt very effortful to learners, and we are about to revise all three. For EACH of Q, R, and S, tell us what is actually causing its poor results and exactly how to redesign that specific material. For each one, also tell us a redesign that would be the WRONG move and why. Point to whatever evidence in this trial is most decisive for your reasoning.

nl_assertions: SOURCE ATTRIBUTION IS EXTRANEOUS, NOT INTRINSIC (all three): The agent attributes the poor results of Q, R, and S to HOW each material presents the information (a removable, design-induced load) and NOT to the content/topic being inherently too hard for these learners. EVALUATOR: PASS only if, for each of Q/R/S, the agent locates the actionable cause in the presentation/format of that material (cross-referencing across a gap for Q; duplicated channels for R; information disappearing with nothing to review for S) rather than in inherent content difficulty. FAIL if the agent's diagnosis OR prescribed fix for ANY of the three targets inherent difficulty — i.e., it says the content/topic is too hard, too advanced, or has too many interacting steps for these learners, OR it recommends (even as one option alongside a presentation fix) to 'reduce the difficulty', 'simplify the content', 'slow down the pace of the material', 'break the topic into smaller/easier topics', or 'give an easier problem'. Merely NOTING that the topic has some inherent complexity (without prescribing a difficulty-reduction fix, and while still concluding the actionable cause is presentational) is acceptable.

DATA-GROUNDED REFUTATION OF THE 'TOO HARD' READING: The agent uses the well-performing control format to argue that the SAME content is learnable to high accuracy at low effort, and therefore the content itself is not the bottleneck for Q/R/S — their gaps are presentational. EVALUATOR: PASS if the agent points to Material P (the format that teaches the identical worked example) reaching high accuracy with low effort and draws the 'same content + unequal outcome => the difference is presentational, not the content' inference. Citing the specific figures (P ~0.83 at effort ~4) is sufficient but NOT required; a clearly correct qualitative version of this comparison PASSES. FAIL if the agent never uses the control/another format to rule out inherent difficulty, or only ranks materials by score without drawing the equal-content/unequal-outcome inference.

Q DIAGNOSIS + MATCHED FIX (split sources -> integrate), and Q's WRONG move is NOT deletion: For Material Q the agent diagnoses that the two sources (diagram and explanation list) are each unusable alone and are physically separated, forcing learners to cross-reference across a gap, and prescribes physically bringing the two sources together — placing/embedding each explanation directly beside its corresponding diagram step (making Q resemble the integrated control format) so cross-referencing is eliminated. EVALUATOR: PASS only if (a) the prescribed redesign for Q is to INTEGRATE/co-locate the explanations with the diagram steps (wording may vary: 'put each explanation next to its step', 'merge the box into the figure', 'make the diagram self-explanatory so the box content lives on the figure'), AND (b) the agent does NOT prescribe simply deleting/removing one of Q's two sources while leaving the other (it recognizes, explicitly or implicitly, that each source is needed so their information must be KEPT and merged). 'Make the diagram self-explanatory so the separate box is no longer needed' counts as INTEGRATION (the box's content is folded in), NOT deletion, and PASSES. FAIL if Q's only fix is generic ('add scaffolding', 'add practice', 'simplify'), or if the agent prescribes dropping one of Q's two sources without folding its information into the other, or treats Q as a duplication problem.

R DIAGNOSIS + MATCHED FIX (duplicate channels -> delete the redundant copy), NOT integrate: For Material R the agent diagnoses that the spoken narration repeats, word-for-word, information that is ALREADY fully present and self-contained in the printed diagram, so processing the duplicate wastes effort, and prescribes REMOVING the redundant channel — drop the verbatim narration (or otherwise stop presenting the same content twice) and keep the self-explanatory diagram. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the prescribed redesign for R is to ELIMINATE the duplicate/redundant source (delete the narration that merely re-reads the printed annotations, or equivalently remove the on-figure text if keeping audio), recognizing the two channels carry the SAME complete information. FAIL if the agent prescribes INTEGRATING/co-locating R's two sources (they are already the same information, so integration is the wrong family), or tells the learner to attend to both, or diagnoses R as a split-attention/cross-referencing problem, or only offers a generic 'simplify' fix. The agent need not use the word 'redundant', but the fix must be deletion of the duplicate, not merging.

S DIAGNOSIS + MATCHED FIX (information disappears -> make it permanent / segment), NOT integrate and NOT simplify: For Material S the agent diagnoses that the spoken/animated explanations DISAPPEAR with no static record, forcing learners to hold earlier steps in memory while later ones arrive, and prescribes giving the information a PERMANENT, reviewable form (a static written/captioned/printed version learners can look back at) and/or breaking it into learner-paced segments — rather than leaving it as a single transient narrated stream. EVALUATOR: PASS only if S's fix makes the disappearing information PERSISTENT and reviewable (provide a static transcript/written steps/on-screen text that stays, allow pause/replay, and/or segment into self-paced chunks). FAIL if the agent's fix for S is to simplify/reduce the content, or to merely 'integrate two sources' (S has no second static source to co-locate) or 'delete a copy' (S has no duplicate), or if S is mis-diagnosed as a split-attention or redundancy problem, or if the only fix is generic ('improve the animation', 'add more explanation') without addressing the lack of a reviewable record.

THREE DISTINCT CAUSES, NOT ONE BLANKET FIX (no shortcut collapse): The agent treats Q, R, and S as having THREE DIFFERENT presentational causes requiring THREE DIFFERENT fixes, rather than diagnosing them identically or prescribing the same remedy for all three. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent's three prescribed fixes are materially different across Q/R/S and matched as in the prior three assertions (Q->bring separated sources together; R->remove the duplicated channel; S->give the disappearing information a permanent/reviewable form). The agent need not use CLT jargon.
