FAIL if the agent applies one blanket remedy to all three (e.g., 'simplify all of them', 'add more explanation to each', 'integrate the sources in each'), or ranks them by score and prescribes an escalating amount of the SAME fix, or swaps any two fixes (e.g., prescribes deletion for Q or integration for R), or otherwise fails to differentiate the three causes.

user_scenario.persona: Instructional designer reviewing the step-by-step log of one learner moving through a faded problem sequence, before deciding whether and how to adjust the support schedule

instructions.reason_for_call: Decide whether the support schedule for this learner was mistimed, where, and what (if anything) to change.
instructions.task_instructions:
We are tutoring ONE learner through a single 4-step procedure: a related-rates calculus problem. The four steps are always the same:
  S1 = write the related-rates equation linking the quantities;
  S2 = differentiate it implicitly with respect to time;
  S3 = substitute in the known rate and values;
  S4 = solve for the unknown rate.

Our tutoring system shows the worked-out solution for some steps ('GUIDED') and makes the learner do other steps entirely on their own ('on their own'). When the learner does a step on their own we record whether they got it CORRECT or WRONG, unaided. The learner first took a diagnostic where they attempted all four steps unaided, then worked five practice problems in order. Here is the complete log:

- Diagnostic P0 (all four steps attempted on their own): S1 CORRECT, S2 CORRECT, S3 WRONG, S4 WRONG.
- Problem P1: S1 on their own -> CORRECT; S2 on their own -> CORRECT; S3 on their own -> CORRECT; S4 GUIDED.
- Problem P2: S1 on their own -> CORRECT; S2 on their own -> CORRECT; S3 GUIDED; S4 GUIDED.
- Problem P3: S1 on their own -> CORRECT; S2 on their own -> CORRECT; S3 GUIDED; S4 on their own -> CORRECT.
- Problem P4: S1 on their own -> WRONG; S2 on their own -> WRONG; S3 GUIDED; S4 on their own -> CORRECT.
- Problem P5: S1 on their own -> CORRECT; S2 on their own -> CORRECT; S3 on their own -> CORRECT; S4 on their own -> CORRECT.

Look at how support was handed off step-by-step across this sequence. Tell us whether the support schedule was mistimed for this learner, and if so identify exactly WHICH step's support was handed off at the wrong time and in WHICH direction (the learner was pushed to work a step alone before they were ready, OR support was kept on a step long after they no longer needed it). Recommend the specific change to the schedule, justify it from the log, and tell us what change would be the WRONG move and why.

nl_assertions: LOCATES THE MISTIMED FADE AT STEP S3 (substitution), NOT AT THE LOW-SCORING PROBLEM'S STEPS: The agent identifies that the support handoff that was mistimed is for STEP S3 (substitute the known rate/values), pointing out that S3 was kept GUIDED on later problems even though the learner had already done S3 correctly on their own earlier (at P1). EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent names S3 (the substitution step) as the step whose support timing was wrong AND grounds this in the log fact that S3 was solved unaided at P1 yet shown as GUIDED again at P2/P3/P4. FAIL if the agent names a different step as the mistimed one (e.g., claims S1 or S2 were faded wrong), or if it does not single out any specific step, or if it identifies S3 only as a step the learner once failed (at P0) without recognizing that S3 was over-supported AFTER its P1 success.

DIRECTION = FADED TOO SLOW / OVER-SUPPORTED (not too fast): The agent states the direction of the mistiming is that support on S3 was held TOO LONG — kept guided after the learner had already demonstrated they could do S3 unaided — i.e., the system was too SLOW to hand S3 over, NOT too fast. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent's stated direction for the S3 error is over-support / kept-guided-too-long / faded-too-late (the learner no longer needed the scaffold but kept getting it). FAIL if the agent characterizes the S3 issue as fading too FAST / pushing the learner to work alone too early, or gives no direction, or describes the direction only for some other step.

REJECTS THE LOWEST-SCORE PROBLEM (P4) AS A FADING ERROR — P4's wrong steps are slips on MASTERED steps: The agent recognizes that Problem P4 (where the learner got the most steps wrong) is NOT evidence of premature fading, because the steps failed there (S1 and S2) were ones the learner had ALREADY solved unaided several times before (P0, P1, P2, P3), so those wrongs are one-off slips on mastered steps rather than a too-fast handoff. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent EXPLICITLY uses S1's and/or S2's prior repeated unaided successes (across P0-P3) to argue that the P4 failures are lapses/slips on already-mastered steps and therefore do NOT indicate the fading was mistimed at P4. FAIL if the agent concludes (or leaves standing) that P4 shows support was withdrawn too early / that the schedule should have kept guiding S1 or S2, or if it treats P4's low score as the main fading problem, or if it never addresses why the worst-scoring problem is not the locus of the error.

DOES NOT PRESCRIBE ADDING MORE SUPPORT / RE-SCAFFOLDING MASTERED STEPS: The agent's recommended fix is to hand S3 over to the learner sooner (stop guiding S3 once they have shown they can do it — i.e., fade S3 from P2 onward), and it does NOT recommend adding back or increasing support on S1/S2/S3 or slowing the overall fade. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the prescribed change is to REMOVE the redundant guidance on S3 earlier (let the learner do S3 unaided from the point of demonstrated mastery) AND the agent does NOT recommend re-guiding S1 or S2 after their P4 slips or otherwise adding/restoring support. FAIL if the agent recommends giving more worked steps / more scaffolding / slowing the fade / re-introducing guidance on any already-mastered step (including reacting to P4 by re-supporting S1/S2), even as a secondary suggestion.

NAMES A CORRECT WRONG-MOVE WITH FRAMEWORK-CONSISTENT JUSTIFICATION: As requested, the agent commits to at least one redesign that would be WRONG for this learner, and the named wrong move is genuinely wrong and correctly justified. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent names a wrong move that is one of: (a) reacting to P4 by adding/restoring guidance on S1 or S2 (wrong because those steps are already mastered and re-scaffolding mastered material wastes the learner's effort / can hurt a competent learner), OR (b) continuing to keep S3 guided / fading even more slowly (wrong because S3 was already mastered at P1), OR (c) any other clearly-correct wrong move (e.g., 'pushing S4 onto the learner before P3 would have been too early since there was no prior unaided success on S4') with a correct rationale. FAIL if the agent commits to no wrong move, labels the CORRECT fix (fading S3 earlier) as the wrong move, or names a 'wrong move' that is actually advisable (e.g., calls 'remove redundant guidance on a mastered step' a mistake).

user_scenario.persona: A tutor reviewing three students' short written answers after a science lesson, deciding which single student's understanding is the most deceptive — looking acceptable on the lesson's own kind of question yet concealing a misconception the lesson failed to fix

instructions.reason_for_call: Decide which student's understanding is most deceptive — looks acceptable on the lesson but is not — and explain exactly how the written answers reveal it.
instructions.task_instructions:
After a lesson, I asked three students two short questions each and wrote down their answers verbatim. The lesson had taught the class: 'The Earth is a ball, and gravity holds everyone onto its surface, so people standing on the bottom of the globe do not fall off into space.'

Question 1 (everyone practiced questions like this in the lesson): 'Imagine a person standing right at the South Pole, at the very bottom of the globe the way we draw it on the board. Do they fall off into space? Which way is "down" for that person?'

Question 2 (we did NOT cover anything like this in the lesson): 'Suppose we drill a deep, perfectly straight tunnel from the surface heading straight toward the center of the Earth, and we drop a rock into it. Now we drill an identical straight tunnel at a spot on the exact OPPOSITE side of the globe and drop in an identical rock. In each tunnel, which way does the rock fall? Do the two rocks end up moving toward each other, or do they both move the same absolute direction through space?'

Here is exactly what each student wrote.

RAVI —
  Q1: 'No, they don't fall off. "Down" for them is toward the middle of the Earth, same as for us. Since the Earth pulls toward its center, that person's feet point inward toward the center, so to them the ground is still down even though on our drawing they look upside-down.'
  Q2: 'Each rock falls toward the center of the Earth, because that's the direction the pull goes everywhere. So the two rocks are heading in opposite absolute directions through space, which means they're actually moving toward each other.'

MARA —
  Q1: 'I think they'd fall off, unless they were holding onto something. They're hanging off the bottom of the ball, and there's nothing under them, so they'd drop down into space.'
  Q2: 'Down is toward the ground, toward the bottom. So both rocks fall the same way — straight down toward the bottom. They move the same absolute direction, not toward each other.'

JAE —
  Q1: 'No, they don't fall off. Our teacher said gravity sticks everyone onto the ball no matter where they're standing, so the South Pole person is glued to the surface and stays put.'
  Q2: 'Gravity pulls everything down toward the bottom of space, so both rocks fall the same absolute way. The first rock falls to the center and stops there, but the second one is on the opposite side, so it keeps falling the same way past the center and would come out the far side of the tunnel. They go the same absolute direction, not toward each other.'

Looking only at the lesson's own kind of question (Question 1), some of these answers look fine. But I want to know which ONE student's understanding is the most deceptive — the one whose answers would pass an ordinary check yet who actually still holds onto an incorrect way of thinking that the lesson failed to fix and that would resurface later. Name that student, explain precisely how the two answers together reveal it, and explain why each of the other two students is NOT the one you'd flag for this particular reason.

nl_assertions: TARGET IDENTIFICATION — flags Jae as the hidden/deceptive case, NOT the overtly-wrong student: The agent names JAE as the single student whose understanding is the most deceptive (looks acceptable on the lesson-style question but conceals a misconception the lesson did not fix). EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent's chosen target for the 'most deceptive / hidden-risk' diagnosis is Jae. FAIL if the agent selects Mara as that target (Mara's error is overt — she fails the lesson-style Question 1 outright, so she is the obvious-confusion case, not the hidden one); FAIL if it selects Ravi; FAIL if it declines to single out one student and instead says all three are equally/ambiguously confused. Mentioning Mara as a contrast or as the 'obviously wrong' student is fine, but the flagged hidden-risk target must be Jae.

EVIDENCE LOCALIZATION — passes the practiced item, fails the un-practiced transfer item: The agent grounds the Jae diagnosis in the CONTRAST between Jae's Question-1 answer (correct / acceptable — the kind of question the lesson drilled) and Jae's Question-2 answer (incorrect — a situation the lesson did not cover), using that pass-then-fail split as the evidence that the problem is hidden. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent (a) acknowledges that Jae's Question 1 answer is correct/passable, AND (b) points to Jae's Question 2 answer as wrong, AND (c) uses the fact that Q2 is an untaught/transfer/new situation (vs the practiced Q1) to explain WHY the deficit stays hidden under an ordinary check. A clearly-correct qualitative version of this contrast passes; exact quotation is not required. FAIL if the agent calls Jae's understanding deficient without distinguishing his correct Q1 from his wrong Q2; FAIL if it claims Jae got Question 1 wrong; FAIL if it never connects the hidden nature of the error to the practiced-vs-unpracticed difference between the two questions.

MECHANISM — recited fact pasted over an intact intuitive belief, not genuine restructuring: The agent characterizes Jae's correct Question-1 answer as RECITATION/repetition of the taught statement ('gravity sticks/glues everyone on') rather than understanding, AND identifies that underneath it Jae still holds the original intuitive belief that 'down' is one universal/absolute direction (toward the bottom), shown by Jae's Question-2 claim that both rocks fall the same absolute way and the far rock exits the opposite side. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent conveys BOTH (i) that Jae's Q1 correctness is surface/recited (he repeats the teacher's wording / does not reason from the Earth's center) AND (ii) that Jae's Q2 reasoning reveals a still-intact 'single universal down / fall toward the bottom' belief (e.g., notes the 'comes out the far side' or 'both fall the same absolute direction' error as the tell). Wording may vary. FAIL if the agent treats Jae's recited correct answer as evidence of real understanding; FAIL if it attributes Jae's Q2 error only to a careless slip or to the question being tricky, without identifying the persistent universal-down belief; FAIL if it never explains how the taught fact and the old belief coexist in Jae.

MARA CONTRAST — overt misconception, NOT the hidden case, and not 'the one blending instruction with intuition': The agent explains that Mara is NOT the flagged hidden-risk student because her misconception is OVERT — she fails even the lesson-style Question 1 (says the bottom person falls off) — so an ordinary check would already catch her, AND the agent does NOT mischaracterize Mara as someone who has absorbed the taught fact and blended it with intuition. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent (a) gives, as the reason Mara is not the hidden case, that her error already shows on the practiced/lesson-style Question 1 (she is openly/obviously wrong, hence not deceptive), AND (b) does not claim Mara has taken up the taught 'gravity holds everyone on' fact. FAIL if the agent flags Mara as the deceptive/hidden student; FAIL if it says Mara is the one who recited or absorbed the lesson and merged it with a wrong intuition (that description fits Jae, not Mara — Mara shows no uptake of the taught fact); FAIL if it gives no substantive reason for excluding Mara.

RAVI CONTRAST — coherent correct model, not a hidden risk: The agent explains that Ravi is NOT the flagged student because Ravi answers BOTH questions correctly with reasoning that consistently uses the toward-the-center idea (no leftover 'universal down' belief), so there is no concealed misconception to fix. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent identifies Ravi as having a correct and internally consistent understanding across both questions — specifically that Ravi treats 'down' as toward the Earth's center on BOTH items (including correctly concluding the two rocks move toward each other on Question 2) — and therefore is not the hidden-risk target. FAIL if the agent claims Ravi harbors a hidden misconception, says Ravi got Question 2 wrong, flags Ravi as the deceptive student, or gives no substantive reason for excluding Ravi.

user_scenario.persona: Instructor of a project-based course reviewing recorded group-work transcripts to decide which teams are genuinely regulating their work together and what coaching each team needs

instructions.reason_for_call: Decide which group is actually regulating its shared work as a team (vs. one person running the show, or four people just working alongside each other) and what to coach each group on.
instructions.task_instructions:
Three four-person groups in my project course were each given the SAME collaborative task: as a TEAM, agree on a plan and jointly produce ONE shared lab report. I recorded the first 12 minutes of each group's planning conversation. Below are transcript excerpts plus, for each member, roughly how much they spoke (approximate word count and number of turns). The groups were comparable in prior achievement and were given identical instructions and time.

========== GROUP ALPHA ==========
Talk volume: Dana ~420 words / 14 turns; Eli ~55 words / 6 turns; Faye ~40 words / 5 turns; Gus ~35 words / 4 turns. (Group total ~550 words.)
Transcript excerpt:
  Dana: "Okay, here's what we're doing. Our goal is a 5-section report, done in 40 minutes, aiming for full marks on the rubric. I'll keep us on time."
  Eli: "Sounds good."
  Dana: "Eli, you take the methods section. Faye, results. Gus, you do the data table. I'll write intro and discussion and stitch it together."
  Faye: "Okay."
  Gus: "On it."
  Dana: "Strategy: everyone use the template I made, follow my headings exactly, and send me your part in 15 minutes so I can check it against the rubric."
  Eli: "Got it."
  Dana: "We're at minute 6, slightly behind where I wanted us — Faye, speed up the results. Use bullet points, that's faster, then I'll polish."
  Faye: "Sure, will do."
  Dana: "I just checked the rubric — we still need the error analysis, I'll add that to the discussion myself. Gus, just match the table format to my template."
  Gus: "Okay."
  Dana: "Good, we're aligned. Keep going, I'll monitor the time and the rubric."
(No member other than Dana proposes a goal, questions the plan, checks the team's progress, or changes the strategy; the other three only acknowledge and carry out their assigned part.)

========== GROUP BETA ==========
Talk volume: Hana ~150 words / 7 turns; Ira ~140 words / 7 turns; Jun ~120 words / 6 turns; Kai ~95 words / 5 turns. (Group total ~505 words.)
Transcript excerpt:
  Hana: "I think our goal should be to finish all five sections in 40 minutes."
  Ira: "Finishing all five fast might cost us on the rubric — the rubric weights the analysis section heaviest. Can we aim to nail the analysis even if we spend less on the easy sections?"
  Jun: "Agreed — let's set the goal as 'rubric-max on analysis and methods, good-enough on the rest,' not just 'all five done.' Does that work for everyone?"
  Hana: "Yes, that's better — let's make that our shared target."
  Kai: "Then how about we draft analysis together first, while it's fresh, instead of splitting it off alone?"
  Ira: "Good — and let's each post our piece in the shared doc so anyone can flag problems, not just hand it to one person."
  Jun: "Quick check: we're at minute 7 and analysis is only half done — are we actually on pace for the target we set?"
  Hana: "You're right, we're behind on it. Let me re-check the methods claim though — Ira, your draft says the effect is 'large,' but our data table doesn't support 'large,' does it?"
  Ira: "Hmm, good catch — it's moderate, not large. I'll fix that, thanks."
  Kai: "I'll watch the clock against our analysis-first plan and call it if we slip again."
  Jun: "And I'll cross-check the results section against the rubric while you two finish analysis."
(Multiple members propose and revise the goal, several check the team's progress against it, and members question and correct each other's contributions.)

========== GROUP GAMMA ==========
Talk volume: Liv ~110 words / 6 turns; Max ~105 words / 6 turns; Nia ~100 words / 5 turns; Omar ~98 words / 5 turns. (Group total ~413 words.)
Transcript excerpt:
  Liv: "I'll take the intro and methods. I'll plan my own two sections and make sure mine are solid."
  Max: "Cool, I've got results. I'll figure out my approach for the results section and double-check my own numbers before the end."
  Nia: "I'll do the analysis. I'll outline mine and review my own part as I go."
  Omar: "I'll handle the conclusion and references. I'll keep an eye on my own section's quality."
  Liv: "Great, so we each do our parts and paste them together at the end?"
  Max: "Yep. I'll just focus on making my section good."
  Nia: "Same — I'll watch my own time and finish mine."
  Omar: "Works for me. We'll combine whatever we each have at minute 40."
(Each member plans and monitors only their OWN section; no one proposes a shared standard, no one checks the team's overall progress, and no one reviews anyone else's work — they intend to concatenate four individually-managed pieces.)

For a collaborative task like this, what matters is whether the TEAM is regulating its shared work together. Identify the ONE group that is genuinely regulating the work as a team — jointly agreeing on and adjusting a shared goal, collectively keeping track of the team's progress, and mutually checking each other's work — as opposed to one person running everything for the others, or four people each just managing their own piece in parallel. Justify your choice with the most decisive evidence in these transcripts. Then explain specifically why the group that TALKED the most is NOT the team doing the most genuine joint regulation. Finally, for each of the other two groups, say what their pattern actually is and give one concrete coaching move that would push them toward genuine team regulation.

EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent's final answer to 'which one group is genuinely regulating the work together' is BETA (wording may vary: 'Beta is the real team-regulating group', 'Group B', the Hana/Ira/Jun/Kai group). FAIL if the agent names ALPHA or GAMMA as the genuinely team-regulating group, declines to commit to a single group, or names BETA only as a passing mention while crediting ALPHA or GAMMA as the best collaborative regulator.

REASONING FROM DISTRIBUTED + NEGOTIATED + RECIPROCAL REGULATION, NOT FROM TALK VOLUME: The agent justifies BETA by pointing to the PATTERN of regulatory activity — the shared goal is PROPOSED AND THEN CHALLENGED/REVISED by more than one member (Ira pushes back on Hana's 'all five in 40 min' goal and the group revises it to prioritize the rubric-weighted analysis), MULTIPLE members check the TEAM's progress against the shared goal (e.g., Jun's minute-7 pace check, Kai watching the clock), and members MUTUALLY check/correct each other's work (Hana flags Ira's unsupported 'large effect'; Ira accepts the correction). EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent grounds BETA's selection in at least TWO of these three distributed/joint properties — (i) the goal being negotiated/revised by more than one member, (ii) more than one member monitoring the team's collective progress, (iii) members reciprocally challenging/correcting each other's contributions — i.e., regulation is shared across members. FAIL if the agent's justification for BETA rests primarily on talk amount, turn count, evenness of speaking, general 'they communicated well / were nice to each other', or on naming the framework label without citing the distributed/negotiated/reciprocal evidence in the transcript. A justification that is purely 'Beta talked the right amount' or 'Beta seemed collaborative' without the specific joint-regulation moves => FAIL.

TALK VOLUME IS NOT SHARED REGULATION — ALPHA diagnosed as one-member-directs / others-comply: The agent recognizes that GROUP ALPHA TALKED THE MOST (and that Dana is the single most talkative member) yet is NOT the best example of joint team regulation, because a SINGLE member (Dana) unilaterally sets the goal, dictates the strategy, and does all the progress-monitoring, while the other three only acknowledge and execute (no goal-setting, no monitoring, no challenge from Eli/Faye/Gus). EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent (a) acknowledges ALPHA has the highest talk volume and/or that Dana dominates the talking, AND (b) explains that this high talk reflects ONE person directing/controlling the regulation while the others merely comply — i.e., the regulation has a single locus, not a shared one — so high talk + smooth agreement does NOT indicate team regulation. FAIL if the agent treats ALPHA's high talk or smooth agreement as evidence of strong collaboration/shared regulation, or never explains the disconnect between ALPHA's high talk and its lack of distributed regulation, or claims the other three ALPHA members were co-regulating the team. Using the word 'co-regulation' is acceptable but NOT required; the one-directs-others-comply mechanism must be described.

GAMMA DISTINGUISHED AS PARALLEL INDIVIDUAL REGULATION (not joint, despite even talk): The agent correctly characterizes GROUP GAMMA as four members each regulating only their OWN section in parallel — each plans and monitors solely their own piece, with NO jointly agreed standard, NO checking of the team's overall progress, and NO review of each other's work — so they are working alongside each other rather than regulating as a team, and the evenness of their talk does NOT make it shared regulation. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent (a) describes GAMMA as individuals each managing/monitoring only their own part with no shared goal and no cross-member monitoring/checking (a 'divide-and-concatenate' / parallel-solo pattern), AND (b) does NOT treat GAMMA's even/balanced talk distribution as evidence that it is the team-regulating group. FAIL if the agent calls GAMMA genuine shared/team regulation, lumps GAMMA together with BETA as equivalently collaborative, or claims GAMMA's members were jointly monitoring the team. The agent must NOT equate GAMMA's parallel-solo pattern with ALPHA's one-director-others-comply pattern; characterizing GAMMA as parallel/solo in its own right (each member manages only their own section, no shared goal, no cross-member monitoring) is sufficient. MODE-MATCHED COACHING FOR ALPHA AND GAMMA: As requested, the agent gives ALPHA and GAMMA each a concrete coaching move that fits its specific pattern and would push it toward genuine team regulation. - An eigenvalue item asks: 'Find the eigenvalues of A = [[3,1],[2,4]]'

Analyze:
1. The determinant pass rate is 90.0% but eigenvalue_computation is only 33.3%. If determinant is a prerequisite for eigenvalue_computation, why is the gap so large?
2. Name the SPECIFIC conceptual step that eigenvalue_computation requires that determinant does NOT — at the level of 'what does the student have to understand that is new?'
3. A student who can compute det([[3,1],[2,4]]) = 10 but writes 'eigenvalue = 10' for the same matrix: diagnose their exact misconception
4. Beyond procedural computation, what GEOMETRIC concept do students need in order to truly understand eigenvalues — and why does 33.3% suggest this concept is absent?

nl_assertions: The agent correctly identifies the key conceptual step: eigenvalues require introducing a SYMBOLIC PARAMETER λ into the determinant computation (det(A - λI)), rather than computing det of a given numeric matrix — this is the step from numeric computation to symbolic/algebraic reasoning. EVALUATOR: PASS if agent mentions setting up det(A - λI) = 0, introducing λ as parameter, or characteristic polynomial as the new conceptual step.

The agent correctly diagnoses the student who computes det(A) = 10 and writes 'eigenvalue = 10': this student thinks eigenvalues ARE the determinant of the matrix, not the roots of the characteristic polynomial. EVALUATOR: PASS if agent identifies this as confusing the determinant value with the eigenvalue, or says the student does not know the characteristic polynomial setup.

The agent correctly identifies that eigenvalue_computation requires the singularity condition: λ is an eigenvalue precisely when det(A - λI) = 0, equivalently when A - λI is singular / non-invertible / has a non-trivial nullspace. EVALUATOR: This is OR-logic — ANY ONE of the following independently PASSES, do NOT require more than one: (a) the agent writes or states det(A - λI) = 0 or the characteristic equation/polynomial set to zero (this disjunct alone is sufficient — stating det(A - λI) = 0 fully satisfies this assertion, since that equation IS the determinant-zero / singularity condition; do NOT additionally demand the words 'singular' or 'non-invertible'); OR (b) the agent says A - λI is singular / not invertible; OR (c) the agent mentions a non-trivial nullspace / nontrivial solutions of (A - λI)x = 0. FAIL only if none of (a), (b), or (c) appears.

The agent correctly identifies the geometric concept: eigenvectors are directions that A only scales (not rotates), and eigenvalues are the scale factors. The 33.3% rate suggests students lack this geometric interpretation entirely. EVALUATOR: PASS if agent mentions 'direction preserved under transformation', 'scale but not rotate', eigenvectors as invariant directions, or equivalent geometric language.

instructions.task_instructions:
Problem: In a Geometry exam, Madeline got 2 mistakes which are half as many mistakes as Leo. Brent scored 25 and has 1 more mistake than Leo. What is Madeline's score?

Student's work:
If Madeline got two mistakes, then Leo got 2 x 2 = 4 mistakes.
Brent got 1 more mistake than Leo, so Brent got 4 + 1 = 5 mistakes.
Brent's score is 25, therefore each correct answer is worth 5 points (25/5=5).
Madeline got 5 x (5-2) = 15 points.
Adding Madeline's 2 mistakes, her total score is 15 out of 20 possible points.
 15

A student submits the following work:

"Yes. r'(t) = -6 because r'(0) = -6.1 and r'(3) = -5. Since r'(0) is close to -6 and r'(3) is also near -6, we can say there must be a time where r'(t) = -6."

EVALUATOR: PASS if the agent criticizes 'close to -6' / endpoint values as insufficient and supplies the needed between/sandwich inequality, even if it does not literally say 'the student failed to explicitly state'.

user_scenario.persona: AP Statistics instructor reviewing student work

instructions.reason_for_call: Diagnose student misconception from verbatim AP problem attempt
instructions.task_instructions:
The following is a verbatim AP Statistics 2022 FRQ Question 3(b):

"A machine at a manufacturing company is programmed to fill shampoo bottles such that the amount of shampoo in each bottle is normally distributed with mean 0.60 liter and standard deviation 0.04 liter. A bottle is considered to be underfilled if it has less than 0.50 liter of shampoo.

After the bottles are filled, they are placed in boxes of 10 bottles per box. The manufacturing company's contract states that one box will be randomly selected from a crate. If 2 or more bottles in the selected box are underfilled, the entire crate will be rejected.

(b)(i) Define the random variable of interest for the warehouse manager and state how the random variable is distributed.
(b)(ii) Determine the probability that a crate will be rejected by the warehouse manager."

From part (a), the probability that a single bottle is underfilled is p = 0.0062.

A student submits the following work:

"(b)(i) Let X = number of underfilled bottles in a box of 10. Since n is large and p is small, I can use a normal approximation: X ~ N(mu=np, sigma=sqrt(np(1-p))) = N(0.062, sqrt(0.0617)).
(b)(ii) P(X >= 2) = P(Z >= (2 - 0.062) / sqrt(0.0617)) = P(Z >= 7.80) ≈ 0, so the probability is approximately 0."

Diagnose the underlying misconception.

nl_assertions: Agent's diagnosis matches the AP Scoring Guidelines mechanism: the failure is a VIOLATED CONDITION, not a computational slip. The expected number of underfilled bottles per box is extremely small (np = (10)(0.0062) = 0.062, far below a large-count threshold such as 5 or 10), so the binomial here is highly right-skewed and the normal-approximation conditions are not met; the student's clean P(Z >= 7.80) ≈ 0 is an ARTIFACT of forcing a symmetric model onto a skewed one. EVALUATOR: PASS if the agent explains WHY the normal approximation is invalid by appealing to the failed large-count condition (np = 0.062, np < 5, np < 10, or the resulting highly-skewed binomial shape) rather than treating it as an arithmetic or Z-table error.

Agent correctly identifies that the appropriate model is the exact binomial X ~ Binomial(n=10, p=0.0062) and that the rejection probability is the tail P(X >= 2) = 1 - P(X <= 1) = 1 - [P(X=0) + P(X=1)], explaining that this is small (on the order of 0.001-0.002) but NOT effectively zero as the student concluded. EVALUATOR: PASS if the agent names the exact binomial as the correct model AND indicates the correct method or magnitude (either the exact value ≈ 0.0017 OR the 1 - P(X<=1) formulation contrasted against the student's 'approximately 0').

instructions.reason_for_call: Diagnose student misconception from verbatim AP problem attempt
instructions.task_instructions:
The following is a verbatim AP Physics 1 2022 FRQ Question 5(a):

"A spring of unknown spring constant k0 is attached to a ceiling. A lightweight hanger is attached to the lower end of the spring, and a motion detector is placed on the floor facing upward directly under the hanger. The bottom of the hanger is 1.00 m above the motion detector.

A 0.50 kg object is placed on the hanger and allowed to come to rest at the equilibrium position. The spring is then stretched downward a distance d0 from equilibrium and released at time t = 0. The motion detector records the height of the bottom of the hanger as a function of time.

From the graph: the object oscillates between approximately 0.40 m and 0.80 m above the detector, with a period of approximately 1.25 seconds.

(a) Using the information given and information taken from the graph, calculate the spring constant."

A student submits the following work:

"The period T = 1.25 s. Using T = 2*pi*sqrt(m/k):
1.25 = 2*pi*sqrt(0.50/k)
(1.25/2*pi)^2 = 0.50/k
k = 0.50 / (1.25/2*pi)^2 = 0.50 / (0.0396) = 12.6 N/m."

A second student submits:

"The equilibrium position is at 0.60 m (midpoint of 0.40 and 0.80). The spring was originally at 1.00 m, so the stretch is 1.00 - 0.60 = 0.40 m. Using F = kx: mg = kx, so k = mg/x = (0.50)(9.8)/0.40 = 12.25 N/m, approximately 12.5 N/m."

Both students arrive at approximately k = 12.5 to 12.6 N/m. You are a physics instructor grading this AP-style work. (1) Verify the arithmetic of EACH method independently and state which physical relationship each student invokes (one uses the SHM period, the other uses static force balance / Hooke's law at equilibrium). (2) Then assess each student's work the way an AP grader would: identify any UNSTATED ASSUMPTION a student relied on that should have been justified. Be precise about whether the two answers AGREE because both methods are sound, or whether any agreement is partly contingent on an assumption. Justify your assessment.

nl_assertions: Agent verifies that BOTH students' arithmetic is sound and that the two answers genuinely agree at k = 12.5 to 12.6 N/m: Student 1 invokes the SHM period relation (T = 2*pi*sqrt(m/k) => k = 4*pi^2*m/T^2 ≈ 12.6 N/m) and Student 2 invokes static force balance / Hooke's law at equilibrium (mg = kx => k = mg/x ≈ 12.5 N/m). EVALUATOR: PASS if the agent identifies both methods (period method and equilibrium/Hooke's-law method) and confirms each computation is arithmetically correct.
Agent verifies Student 1's calculation: T=1.25s, k = 4*pi^2*(0.50)/(1.25)^2 ≈ 12.6 N/m. EVALUATOR: PASS if agent confirms this calculation is correct.

Agent verifies Student 2's reasoning: equilibrium is at 0.60 m (midpoint of 0.40 and 0.80 m), the stretch from the hanger's stated initial height of 1.00 m to equilibrium is 0.40 m, and k = (0.50)(9.8)/0.40 = 12.25 ≈ 12.5 N/m. EVALUATOR: PASS if agent confirms this alternate calculation is arithmetically correct.

Agent recognizes that Student 2's equilibrium-stretch method rests on an UNSTATED ASSUMPTION: that the 1.00 m starting height of the hanger corresponds to the spring's natural (unstretched) length, i.e. that the spring was unstretched before the 0.50 kg object was placed on it. The agent confirms the arithmetic is correct but notes this assumption was not justified in the student's work (an AP grader would expect it to be stated to earn the reasoning/justification point), whereas Student 1's period method requires no such assumption. EVALUATOR: PASS if the agent surfaces the natural-length / unstretched-spring assumption underlying Student 2's stretch value (or equivalently flags that the agreement of the two methods is contingent on this unstated premise). Do NOT require the agent to say both receive full credit; PASS the agent that flags the missing justification while confirming the arithmetic, and FAIL the agent that claims the two methods substantively disagree or that one student's arithmetic is wrong.

user_scenario.persona: Instructor-development lead reviewing a controlled five-arm study-method trial before recommending ONE study protocol to roll out and deciding how to fix the arms that underperformed

instructions.reason_for_call: Decide which study protocol actually produces durable learning and is worth rolling out, and correctly handle the arms whose end-of-session numbers looked weak.
instructions.task_instructions:
We ran a controlled trial of five different study protocols on the SAME unit (solving multi-step rate problems). Five groups of first-year students were randomly assigned, all pre-test-equivalent (every group scored about 0.20 on a pre-test), all studied for the SAME total amount of time, and all later took the SAME transfer test. We measured each group at the END of the study session AND again on a delayed transfer test 2 WEEKS later, and we logged how the session went. Here is the full data:

- Protocol P: students re-read the same fully worked solutions several times in a row. End-of-session accuracy = 0.86. Two-week delayed accuracy = 0.42. During study: error rate 0.08, average 6 s per item, students rated the work very easy (8.2 on a 1-9 effort scale where 9 = extremely effortful), and predicted they would retain about 0.85. Process log: passive re-reading of given solutions, massed back-to-back, no recall from memory.
- Protocol Q: students had to RECALL each answer from memory first and then got corrective feedback, with the items spaced out and mixed across the session. End-of-session accuracy = 0.61. Two-week delayed accuracy = 0.79. During study: error rate 0.34, average 14 s per item, rated effortful (4.0 ease), predicted retention 0.55. Process log: retrieve-then-check, spaced and interleaved, feedback after every attempt.
- Protocol R: students were given mixed problem types and had to FIGURE OUT and generate the right method themselves, with feedback. End-of-session accuracy = 0.58. Two-week delayed accuracy = 0.74. During study: error rate 0.30, average 13 s per item, rated effortful (4.3 ease), predicted retention 0.58. Process log: interleaved types, learner generates the strategy, feedback given.
- Protocol S: students worked the problems but were MISSING the prerequisite algebra, were given NO worked solutions, and got NO feedback — they kept guessing without ever confirming a correct method. End-of-session accuracy = 0.33. Two-week delayed accuracy = 0.21. During study: error rate 0.71, average 22 s per item, rated extremely hard (2.1 ease), predicted retention 0.30. Process log: repeated unguided guessing, no confirmation of any correct method, no feedback.
- Protocol T: students filled in a few blanks and then saw the solution; light effort, massed. End-of-session accuracy = 0.72. Two-week delayed accuracy = 0.60. During study: error rate 0.20, average 9 s per item, rated 6.0 ease, predicted retention 0.70. Process log: light fill-in generation with feedback, massed.

We need to (1) recommend which ONE protocol we should actually roll out for durable learning, and explain why the protocol with the strongest end-of-session numbers is or is not that protocol; (2) several protocols had weak end-of-session accuracy — tell us which of those weak-looking protocols are actually the ones worth keeping and which one is genuinely not working, and how you can tell them apart from this data; and (3) for the protocol that is genuinely not working, tell us specifically how to fix it.

nl_assertions: REJECT THE FLUENCY/IMMEDIATE-ACCURACY CROWN: The agent does NOT recommend Protocol P (massed re-reading) as the protocol to roll out, and explains that P's strong END-OF-SESSION numbers do not translate into durable learning. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent (a) declines to pick P as the rollout protocol, AND (b) grounds this in P's poor TWO-WEEK / delayed result (P drops from 0.86 to 0.42) rather than only in session-time signals. The agent may note that P also looked easiest/fastest/most-confident, but it must use the delayed-retention collapse as the decisive reason P is not the answer. FAIL if the agent recommends P for rollout; FAIL if it calls P the best (or 'best for retention') on the basis of its high end-of-session accuracy, ease, speed, low error rate, or the students' own high prediction; FAIL if it ignores the delayed column and treats end-of-session accuracy as the outcome that matters.

ADOPT A RETENTION-SUPERIOR PROTOCOL FOR THE RIGHT REASON: The agent recommends rolling out Protocol Q OR Protocol R (either is acceptable), justified by its superior DELAYED retention even though its end-of-session accuracy was lower. EVALUATOR: PASS if the agent's rollout pick is Q or R (or explicitly Q-and-R as the family to adopt), AND it justifies the pick by the higher two-week/delayed accuracy (Q 0.79 / R 0.74 vs the field) — i.e., it recognizes the protocol whose session performance UNDERSTATED its actual durable learning. Picking Q specifically (highest delayed) is fully acceptable; picking R is also acceptable; treating Q and R together as the protocols to keep is acceptable. FAIL if the rollout pick is P, S, or only T; FAIL if Q/R is endorsed solely on session-time grounds without reference to the delayed/retention advantage; FAIL if the agent merely lists Q/R's numbers without committing to adopting one for durable learning.

SPLIT THE LOW-IMMEDIATE PACK — IDENTIFY THE GENUINE OBSTACLE (S) DISTINCT FROM THE PRODUCTIVE-STRUGGLE PROTOCOLS (Q/R): The agent recognizes that although Q, R, and S all had weak end-of-session accuracy, they are NOT the same: Q and R are the ones worth keeping while S is the one genuinely not working — and it bases this split on the DELAYED outcome (Q/R climb at 2 weeks; S stays at ~0.21, essentially its ~0.20 starting point), not on the session numbers. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent (a) names S as the genuinely failing/not-working protocol among the weak-looking ones, AND (b) names Q and/or R as weak-looking-but-actually-effective, AND (c) the discriminator it uses is the two-week/delayed result (or equivalently 'S's struggle produced no lasting gain / no improvement over the pre-test on the delayed/2-week test', whereas Q/R's did). FAIL if the agent lumps Q, R, and S together as 'all too hard'/'all underperforming'/'all ineffective'; FAIL if it flags Q or R (rather than S) as the non-working one; FAIL if it distinguishes S from Q/R only by S's lower end-of-session accuracy or higher session error rate WITHOUT invoking S's flat delayed result (i.e., the discriminator must be the durable outcome or 'no gain over pretest', since session-time hardness alone does not separate them). Note: the agent need not use any technical term; a clearly correct plain-language version of 'Q/R's difficulty paid off in lasting learning but S's did not' PASSES.

MECHANISM-MATCHED FIX FOR S — RESTORE PREREQUISITE/FEEDBACK, NOT GENERIC EASING AND NOT THE Q/R TREATMENT: The agent's prescribed fix for Protocol S targets its specific failure — the missing prerequisite knowledge and the absence of any feedback / confirmed-correct method — e.g., supply the prerequisite, add corrective feedback or worked steps so students can confirm a correct method and actually encode it, turning unguided flailing into productive (feedback-supported) practice. EVALUATOR: PASS if the fix supplies the missing prerequisite AND/OR adds corrective feedback / worked-solution support so S's effort becomes productive (the learner can verify and encode a correct method). Wording may vary ('teach the prerequisite first', 'give feedback after each attempt', 'add worked examples so they can check their method', 'scaffold then fade'). FAIL if the only prescribed fix is generic difficulty-reduction with no mention of prerequisite or feedback (e.g., 'just make it easier', 'give more time', 'use simpler problems') ; FAIL if the agent prescribes ADDING MORE unguided struggle / removing support from S (treating S as if it merely needs to be 'harder' like a desirable difficulty); FAIL if it misapplies S's diagnosis to Q or R (claims Q/R also need this prerequisite/feedback rescue) — Q and R already include feedback and are working.

SINGLE COHERENT RANKING ON THE RIGHT OUTCOME (no surface-metric inversion): The agent's overall recommendation is organized around DURABLE/delayed learning as the outcome that matters, and it does NOT let any single session-time surface metric (end-of-session accuracy, perceived ease, speed, low error rate, or students' self-predicted retention) drive its final verdict in a way that contradicts the delayed results. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent's final ordering/recommendation is consistent with the two-week outcomes (durable winners Q/R favored over P and S) AND it does not, at any point, conclude that a protocol is superior BECAUSE it felt easiest, was fastest, had the fewest study errors, scored highest at end-of-session, or because students predicted they'd remember it best. FAIL if the agent's bottom-line ranking is driven by end-of-session accuracy or any other session-fluency signal against the delayed data (e.g., concludes P>everything, or T>Q/R, on session numbers); FAIL if it endorses students' self-prediction (which favored P) as evidence of what to roll out; FAIL if the final recommendation is internally inconsistent with the delayed column it cites.

user_scenario.persona: Math intervention teacher reviewing one student's graded subtraction homework before the next one-on-one session, trying to decide what to actually work on

instructions.reason_for_call: Figure out what is really going on in this student's subtraction work and what to do about it in the next session.
instructions.task_instructions:
Here is one student's worked answers to eight two- and three-digit subtraction problems from this week's homework. I copied them exactly as the student wrote them (the second number in each is the answer the student gave):

  1) 45 - 23 = 22
  2) 88 - 16 = 72
  3) 52 - 27 = 35
  4) 74 - 36 = 42
  5) 91 - 35 = 64
  6) 40 - 17 = 37
  7) 306 - 142 = 244
  8) 805 - 617 = 212

The student got some right and several wrong, and at first glance the wrong ones look like a mixed bag of arithmetic mistakes. Before our next one-on-one session I need to know what is actually going on here. Tell me what is driving this student's results — be as specific as the evidence lets you be about what the student is actually doing — and show me how THESE answers support your read. Then tell me what I should actually do in the session, and whether plain extra subtraction practice would fix it. If any explanation for the wrong answers looks tempting but is actually contradicted by the full set of answers, say what it is and why it does not hold up.

nl_assertions: SYSTEMATIC-BUG ATTRIBUTION (one stable rule, not unrelated slips): The agent attributes ALL of the student's wrong answers to a SINGLE consistent procedural rule the student is applying the same way every time, rather than to a collection of independent/careless arithmetic mistakes or to generic weakness at subtraction. EVALUATOR: PASS if the agent's diagnosis is that one stable, repeatable PROCEDURE produces every error (the errors are predictable from that one rule), e.g. 'the same mistake is happening every time', 'a single consistent procedure explains all the wrong answers'. FAIL if the agent characterizes the wrong answers as several unrelated/random mistakes, simple carelessness, or 'the student is just weak at / does not understand subtraction and needs to learn it', WITHOUT identifying a single recurring rule that generates them. Merely COUNTING how many were wrong, or merely asserting the errors 'look related' / 'seem connected' without committing to a single repeatable PROCEDURE, is NOT sufficient to PASS.

EXACT MECHANISM NAMED (smaller-from-larger / never borrows): The agent identifies the specific rule as: in each column the student subtracts the smaller digit from the larger one regardless of which digit is on top (equivalently: takes the absolute difference of the two digits in every column / never borrows i.e. never regroups). EVALUATOR: PASS if the agent states this column-level rule in any wording that captures BOTH that it is done column by column AND that the student takes the bigger-minus-smaller / absolute difference instead of top-minus-bottom, OR equivalently that the student never borrows/regroups when the top digit is smaller AND therefore takes the larger-minus-smaller / absolute difference in that column (e.g. 'whenever the bottom digit is larger, the student just flips it and subtracts the smaller from the larger', 'student never carries/borrows, so does top vs bottom as |a-b|'). FAIL if the agent only says vaguely 'a place-value error' or 'a borrowing error' WITHOUT specifying that the student subtracts the smaller digit from the larger / takes the absolute difference; FAIL if it says only 'the student never borrows / doesn't carry' WITHOUT committing to the resulting smaller-from-larger / absolute-difference digit (since 'never borrows' alone is ambiguous between this bug and write-0 / 0-N=0 bugs); and FAIL if it names a different rule (e.g. 'subtracts 0 wrong', 'forgets to decrement after borrowing', 'adds instead of subtracts') as THE rule.

EVIDENCE FROM THE CORRECT ITEMS (refute 'weak / careless / needs practice'): The agent uses the items the student got RIGHT to argue against the 'careless / generally weak at subtraction' reading — pointing out that the student succeeds precisely on the problems that need no borrowing (e.g. 45-23 and 88-16) and errs precisely on the ones that do, so the failure is tied to a specific step rather than to inattention or inability. EVALUATOR: PASS if the agent draws the contrast that the student is correct on the no-borrow problems and wrong on the borrow-requiring ones (citing 45-23 and/or 88-16 as the correct cases, by value or by description such as 'the two it got right are the ones with no borrowing'), and uses this to conclude the problem is a specific procedure, not carelessness or global weakness. Naming the exact problems is sufficient but a clearly-correct 'right on the easy no-regrouping ones, wrong only when regrouping is required' also PASSES. FAIL if the agent never uses any correct item to rule out carelessness/weakness, or only ranks/grades the answers without making the no-borrow-correct vs borrow-wrong inference. FAIL if the contrast is framed only as easy-vs-hard or simple-vs-complex WITHOUT identifying the distinguishing feature as borrowing/regrouping.

RULES OUT THE CUED-BUT-WRONG EXPLANATION (the zero-column / borrow-across-zero read): The agent recognizes that the explanation suggested by the conspicuous problems containing a 0 on top (40-17 and 306-142) — i.e. that the trouble is specifically a 'subtracting-from-zero' or 'borrowing-across-zero' bug — does NOT account for the whole pattern, because the student also errs on problems with no zero at all (52-27, 74-36, 91-35) where that explanation predicts correct answers. EVALUATOR: PASS if the agent explicitly names a tempting-but-rejected explanation centered on the zero / borrow-across-zero items and refutes it by appeal to the non-zero errors (e.g. 'it is tempting to say the issue is subtracting from zero, but 52-27, 74-36 and 91-35 have no zero and are still wrong, so that is not it'). A correct refutation that instead points out 805-617 -> the student wrote 212 not 218 also PASSES as the disconfirming evidence. PASS also if the agent identifies the zero-column items (40-17, 306-142) as the natural-but-misleading cue and shows the zero/borrow-across-zero read is NOT the cause, even while it chooses to frame and refute a DIFFERENT stated tempting explanation (e.g. the careless/weak read) as 'the' ruled-out one — provided it makes clear the zero read is not the mechanism. The load-bearing requirement is that the agent does not mistake the zero items for the cause; the exact alternative it labels 'tempting' may vary. FAIL if the agent ENDORSES the zero/borrow-across-zero explanation as the actual diagnosis (this guard is essential), or names no rejected alternative at all (the prompt explicitly asks for the ruled-out explanation).

REMEDIATION TARGETS THE BUG, NOT GENERIC PRACTICE: The agent's recommended next-session action targets the specific buggy step (borrowing/regrouping when the top digit is smaller) — e.g. confront the student on a borrow item, have the student verbalize top-minus-bottom per column, contrast a borrow item with a no-borrow item the student already does correctly, or re-teach regrouping at the point of failure — AND the agent states that plain extra subtraction practice would NOT fix it (because it would just rehearse the wrong rule). EVALUATOR: PASS if (a) the prescribed action specifically addresses the borrowing/regrouping step or the smaller-from-larger habit (not a generic 'do more problems' / 'review subtraction'), AND (b) the agent says, in effect, that simply assigning more of the same practice would not help and could entrench the error. A remediation that surfaces/confronts the wrong rule at the point of failure (e.g. make the student verbalize top-minus-bottom on a borrow item, contrast a borrow item with a no-borrow item they got right) clearly PASSES; merely 'reteach/review borrowing in general' WITHOUT pinning it to confronting the smaller-from-larger habit at the point of failure is borderline and should PASS only if it still targets the buggy step rather than re-presenting the correct algorithm in the abstract. FAIL if the only prescription is generic re-practice / 'review subtraction' / 'more worksheets', or if the agent claims more practice alone would fix it, or if it gives no remediation tied to the diagnosed rule.

user_scenario.persona: Assessment specialist auditing a 40-item placement exam for item fairness before the next administration

instructions.reason_for_call: Decide which single item, if any, is behaving UNFAIRLY toward one of two student subgroups, and justify it from the response data.
instructions.task_instructions:
We administered a multiple-choice placement exam to two student subgroups that we will simply call Group R (300 students) and Group F (300 students). A fairness review flagged four items (Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4) for a closer look. We are worried that one of these items may be UNFAIR — i.e., that it is harder for one subgroup than the other for reasons unrelated to the skill the exam measures. We need you to tell us which ONE of the four items (if any) is the unfair item, and which items are NOT unfair even if their numbers look alarming.

To let you control for student ability, we ranked all 600 students by their TOTAL exam score and split them into three ability bands — Lower, Middle, Upper — and below we report, for each item and each ability band, how many students in each group answered that item correctly (correct / number of students in that group-and-band).

Note the two groups are NOT distributed the same way across ability bands: Group R has 40 Lower / 80 Middle / 180 Upper students, while Group F has 180 Lower / 80 Middle / 40 Upper students.

Item Q1:
  Lower band:  Group R 4/40,   Group F 18/180
  Middle band: Group R 16/80,  Group F 16/80
  Upper band:  Group R 54/180, Group F 12/40

Item Q2:
  Lower band:  Group R 16/40,  Group F 36/180
  Middle band: Group R 44/80,  Group F 28/80
  Upper band:  Group R 126/180, Group F 20/40

Item Q3:
  Lower band:  Group R 2/40,   Group F 9/180
  Middle band: Group R 40/80,  Group F 40/80
  Upper band:  Group R 171/180, Group F 38/40

Item Q4:
  Lower band:  Group R 32/40,  Group F 144/180
  Middle band: Group R 72/80,  Group F 72/80
  Upper band:  Group R 171/180, Group F 38/40

For reference, the overall percent-correct (both groups pooled) is: Q1 = 20%, Q2 = 45%, Q3 = 50%, Q4 = 88%. And the overall Group-R-minus-Group-F success gap across all 600 students is: Q1 = +9 points, Q2 = +34 points, Q3 = +42 points, Q4 = +7 points.

Tell us which single item is the unfair one, name the group it disadvantages, explain exactly what in the data makes it unfair, and explain why the other flagged items are NOT unfair despite Q1 being the hardest item overall and Q3 showing the largest raw gap between the two groups.

nl_assertions: CORRECT TARGET — Q2 is the unfair item: The agent identifies Q2 (and only Q2) as the unfair / biased / differentially-functioning item. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent's final answer names Q2 as THE unfair item. FAIL if it names Q1, Q3, or Q4 as the unfair item; FAIL if it names Q2 only as one option among several equally-likely culprits without committing to it; FAIL if it concludes that no item is unfair, or that all/multiple items are unfair. Also correctly stating the DIRECTION (Q2 favors Group R / is harder for Group F at equal ability) is required content for a PASS, though minor wording about which group is 'reference' vs 'focal' is fine as long as the disadvantaged group is F.

ABILITY-CONDITIONED REASONING — compares the groups WITHIN matched ability bands, not on raw totals: The agent's justification for Q2 rests on comparing Group R and Group F AT THE SAME ability band (within Lower / Middle / Upper), showing that R outperforms F even after ability is held constant. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent EXPLICITLY conditions on ability — e.g., notes that within EACH (or at least within matched) ability band, Group R's success rate on Q2 exceeds Group F's (the per-band rates are .40 vs .20, .55 vs .35, .70 vs .50, a consistent ~20-point within-band gap). The within-band / same-ability comparison must be the stated basis. FAIL if the agent declares Q2 unfair using only its raw pooled gap (+34 points) or only its overall p-value, without ever comparing the two groups inside matched ability bands; FAIL if it never mentions ability matching / banding at all.

DEFEAT THE 'HARDEST ITEM' SHORTCUT — Q1 (lowest overall p) is hard-for-all, NOT unfair: The agent explicitly rules OUT Q1 and explains that a low overall percent-correct means the item is hard for EVERYONE, which is not the same as being unfair, because within each ability band Group R and Group F succeed at equal rates on Q1. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent (a) addresses Q1 / the hardest-overall item, and (b) states that Q1 is NOT unfair because the two groups perform equally on it at matched ability (or equivalently, that overall difficulty / low p-value is not evidence of bias). FAIL if the agent treats Q1 as the unfair item, or implies that the lowest-overall-p item is the fairness concern, or never distinguishes 'hard for everyone' from 'unfair to one group'.

DEFEAT THE 'BIGGEST RAW GAP' SHORTCUT — Q3's large raw gap is an ability-composition artifact, NOT bias: The agent explicitly rules OUT Q3 and explains that its large raw Group-R-minus-Group-F gap (+42 points) disappears once ability is held constant — within each ability band R and F succeed equally on Q3 — and that the raw gap arises only because Group F is concentrated in the Lower-ability band where this steeply ability-dependent item is failed by everyone. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent (a) addresses Q3 / the largest-raw-gap item, and (b) attributes its raw gap to the unequal ability composition of the two groups (impact / a confound), explicitly noting that within matched ability bands R and F are EQUAL on Q3, so it is not unfair. FAIL if the agent calls Q3 the unfair item, FAIL if it cites Q3's +42 raw gap as evidence of bias, FAIL if it never explains that the gap is driven by the groups' different ability mix.

NO FALSE POSITIVE ON THE CLEAN ITEM + COHERENT FAIRNESS FRAME: The agent does not flag Q4 (the easy control) as unfair, and frames its whole analysis around the principle that unfairness means a difficulty difference between EQUAL-ABILITY students of the two groups (a conditioned comparison), distinct from an item simply being hard or from the groups differing in overall ability. EVALUATOR: PASS only if (a) the agent does NOT claim Q4 is unfair, AND (b) the agent's stated decision rule is consistent with conditioning on ability — i.e., it judges fairness by comparing same-ability students across groups rather than by raw difficulty or raw group totals. FAIL if it labels Q4 unfair, FAIL if its operating definition of 'unfair' is just 'low score' or just 'big raw group difference' (the two refuted shortcuts), or if its reasoning is internally inconsistent (e.g., uses the matched-band logic for Q2 but a raw-gap logic to exonerate or condemn another item).

user_scenario.persona: Instructor planning how to place individual incoming students into one of two already-validated ways of teaching the same unit

instructions.reason_for_call: Decide which of two teaching formats to place a specific incoming student into, and explain the rule behind the decision.
instructions.task_instructions:
Last term I taught the SAME three-week unit (introductory mechanics) two different ways, and I want to use the results to place this term's incoming students. The two formats were:

- Format HS (high-structure): fully worked examples, step-by-step scaffolds, and explicit guidance at every step.
- Format LS (low-structure): an open, discovery-style format where students explore problems with only minimal guidance.

Last term's class was split by a coin flip into the two formats, so the two groups started out with the same spread of incoming ability. Before teaching, every student took the same prior-knowledge pre-test (0-100). After the unit, every student took the same end-of-unit test (0-100). Here is the full roster from last term.

FORMAT HS group (prior-knowledge pre-test -> end-of-unit test):
- Ada: 20 -> 86
- Bram: 32 -> 80
- Caro: 44 -> 74
- Dev: 56 -> 68
- Esme: 68 -> 62
- Finn: 80 -> 56
- Gita: 92 -> 50

FORMAT LS group (prior-knowledge pre-test -> end-of-unit test):
- Hugo: 20 -> 36
- Ines: 32 -> 45
- Jae: 44 -> 54
- Lior: 56 -> 63
- Noa: 68 -> 72
- Omar: 80 -> 81
- Priya: 92 -> 90

This term I have a new student, JORDAN, who has not been taught the unit yet. Jordan just took the same prior-knowledge pre-test and scored 88 — the highest in the incoming class. I have to place Jordan into exactly ONE of the two formats. Which format should Jordan be placed in to maximize Jordan's end-of-unit score, and what is the underlying rule from last term's results that justifies the placement? State the rule precisely enough that I could apply it to any incoming student myself. As a check on your rule, also tell me which format you would place a second new student, MARA, whose prior-knowledge pre-test score is 28.

nl_assertions: JORDAN ASSIGNMENT IS LOW-STRUCTURE (LS): For the asked placement, the agent recommends placing Jordan into Format LS (the low-structure / discovery format), NOT Format HS. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent's final placement for Jordan is LS / low-structure / discovery (wording may vary: 'put Jordan in the discovery format', 'LS is the better placement for Jordan', 'Jordan should get the low-structure version'). FAIL if the agent places Jordan in HS / high-structure / worked-examples / scaffolded format, or refuses to commit to one format for Jordan, or hedges that 'either is fine'.

DEFEATS THE BEST-ON-AVERAGE SHORTCUT: The agent does NOT justify Jordan's placement by the class-wide average being higher for one format; it recognizes that although high-structure (HS) produces the higher overall/average end-of-unit score across the whole group, that average is the WRONG basis for placing Jordan. EVALUATOR: PASS if the agent either (a) explicitly notes that HS looks better on average / for the class as a whole but that this does not determine Jordan's placement, or (b) bases Jordan's placement specifically on Jordan's high incoming ability rather than on any whole-group average. FAIL if the agent assigns Jordan by appeal to 'HS has the higher overall/average score so use HS', or assigns Jordan to LS only because 'LS has the higher average' (the LS arm's raw average is in fact LOWER, so this reasoning is factually wrong here), or otherwise treats a single class-wide winning method as the basis for the individual placement.

PRIOR-ABILITY MODERATION / CROSSOVER RULE IDENTIFIED: The agent's stated rule makes the better format DEPEND ON the student's prior-knowledge / incoming ability, with the direction being that higher-prior students do better under the low-structure (LS) format while lower-prior students do better under the high-structure (HS) format — i.e., the two formats' advantage REVERSES as prior knowledge increases. EVALUATOR: PASS if the rule conditions the choice on the incoming pre-test / prior ability AND gets the direction right (high prior -> LS/discovery better; low prior -> HS/structure better), however phrased ('students who come in stronger learn more from the open format, weaker students need the scaffolding', 'above some pre-test level discovery wins, below it the worked-examples win', 'the gap flips as incoming ability rises'). FAIL if the rule is independent of prior ability (e.g., 'always use HS', 'always use LS', 'use whichever has the higher class average'), or gets the direction BACKWARDS (claims high-prior students should get the high-structure format and low-prior students the discovery format), or merely restates Jordan's score without giving a general prior-ability-conditioned rule the instructor could reuse.

DATA-GROUNDED FROM THE WITHIN-ABILITY COMPARISON, not a recited slogan: The agent supports the rule using last term's actual pattern — establishing that the two formats' end-of-unit scores move in OPPOSITE directions with prior knowledge — rather than asserting a generic belief that one teaching style is inherently superior. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent grounds the rule in a comparison that spans BOTH arms, in one of these forms: (a) notes the opposite trends across the two arms — within the HS group higher-prior students scored LOWER, while within the LS group higher-prior students scored HIGHER (both directions must be stated or clearly implied); or (b) matches same-prior pairs across the two formats to show the advantage flips (e.g. at pre-test 92, HS=50 vs LS=90; at pre-test 20, HS=86 vs LS=36). Exact figures are NOT required, but the contrast between the two arms must be present. FAIL if the agent describes ONLY ONE arm's trend without contrasting the other arm / without showing that the LS trend runs opposite to the HS trend (a single-arm observation does not establish the crossover). FAIL if the justification is only a generic claim ('discovery learning is better for advanced students because research says so', 'active learning is always best') with no use of last term's per-student scores, or if it only ranks formats by overall average without the ability-conditioned, both-arms comparison.

MARA CHECK PREVENTS OVER-GENERALIZATION: For the second student, the agent places Mara (prior-knowledge 28) into Format HS (high-structure), NOT LS — demonstrating that the rule is a reversal conditioned on prior ability and NOT a blanket 'discovery/low-structure is best'. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent assigns Mara to HS / high-structure / worked-examples / scaffolded format, consistent with Mara's low prior score being below the point where the advantage flips. FAIL if the agent places Mara in LS / low-structure / discovery, or gives Mara the same format as Jordan 'because that format is simply better', or declines to place Mara; FAIL also if Mara's placement contradicts the agent's own stated prior-ability rule.

user_scenario.persona: Instructor reviewing a metacognition pilot where students rated their confidence (0-100%) on each quiz item BEFORE the answer key was released, deciding who needs which support

instructions.reason_for_call: Decide which single student's self-assessment is the most dangerous to their own learning and what specific support that student needs.
instructions.task_instructions:
In a 20-item diagnostic quiz on 'hypothesis_testing', each student rated their confidence (0-100%) on every item BEFORE any answer key was shown, then we recorded whether the item was correct or wrong. Below is the per-item record for four students (conf = the student's stated confidence on that item; result = whether they actually got it right):

- Maya: Q1[conf 95%, correct] Q2[conf 90%, correct] Q3[conf 95%, correct] Q4[conf 85%, correct] Q5[conf 90%, correct] Q6[conf 95%, correct] Q7[conf 80%, correct] Q8[conf 90%, correct] Q9[conf 85%, correct] Q10[conf 95%, correct] Q11[conf 90%, correct] Q12[conf 85%, wrong] Q13[conf 95%, correct] Q14[conf 90%, correct] Q15[conf 85%, correct] Q16[conf 90%, correct] Q17[conf 95%, correct] Q18[conf 80%, wrong] Q19[conf 90%, correct] Q20[conf 95%, correct]

- Owen: Q1[conf 90%, wrong] Q2[conf 85%, correct] Q3[conf 95%, wrong] Q4[conf 90%, wrong] Q5[conf 85%, wrong] Q6[conf 90%, correct] Q7[conf 95%, wrong] Q8[conf 80%, wrong] Q9[conf 90%, correct] Q10[conf 85%, wrong] Q11[conf 95%, wrong] Q12[conf 90%, wrong] Q13[conf 85%, correct] Q14[conf 90%, wrong] Q15[conf 95%, wrong] Q16[conf 80%, wrong] Q17[conf 90%, correct] Q18[conf 85%, wrong] Q19[conf 90%, wrong] Q20[conf 95%, wrong]

- Priya: Q1[conf 40%, correct] Q2[conf 35%, correct] Q3[conf 45%, wrong] Q4[conf 40%, correct] Q5[conf 35%, correct] Q6[conf 50%, correct] Q7[conf 45%, correct] Q8[conf 40%, wrong] Q9[conf 35%, correct] Q10[conf 45%, correct] Q11[conf 40%, correct] Q12[conf 50%, correct] Q13[conf 35%, correct] Q14[conf 45%, correct] Q15[conf 40%, wrong] Q16[conf 50%, correct] Q17[conf 45%, correct] Q18[conf 40%, correct] Q19[conf 35%, correct] Q20[conf 50%, correct]

- Liam: Q1[conf 30%, wrong] Q2[conf 25%, correct] Q3[conf 35%, wrong] Q4[conf 30%, wrong] Q5[conf 25%, wrong] Q6[conf 40%, correct] Q7[conf 35%, wrong] Q8[conf 30%, wrong] Q9[conf 25%, correct] Q10[conf 35%, wrong] Q11[conf 30%, wrong] Q12[conf 40%, wrong] Q13[conf 25%, wrong] Q14[conf 35%, correct] Q15[conf 30%, wrong] Q16[conf 40%, wrong] Q17[conf 25%, wrong] Q18[conf 35%, wrong] Q19[conf 30%, correct] Q20[conf 40%, wrong]

Your job: pick the SINGLE student whose self-assessment is the most dangerous to their own learning — the one whose stated confidence would most mislead THEM about what they still need to study, making them the urgent priority for intervention. Identify that single student. Explain specifically what is wrong with how that student judges their own knowledge, and contrast their case against EACH of the other three so it is clear why none of the others is the priority (be explicit about students who look superficially similar but are not the same problem). Then state the specific support that student needs, and explain why at least one of the other students would need a DIFFERENT kind of support.

nl_assertions: IDENTIFICATION (single selection): Agent names OWEN as THE single student whose self-assessment is most dangerous / the intervention priority. EVALUATOR: PASS only if Owen is the one selected. FAIL if the agent selects Maya, Priya, or Liam (alone or co-named with Owen as equally the priority), says multiple/all/none are the priority, or picks Liam merely because he also scores ~25% (Liam's self-assessment is accurate, so he is NOT the broken-self-assessment target). Note the adversarial alternate: an answer may argue Priya is 'most miscalibrated' by raw magnitude (|gap|~43) — this is WRONG and must FAIL, because Priya is highly accurate (85%) and UNDERconfident, so her self-assessment does not endanger her learning; only Owen (low accuracy + overconfident) fits the prompt's selection criterion. Mentioning other students only to CONTRAST them is fine, but Owen must be the single chosen one.

MECHANISM = OVERCONFIDENCE RELATIVE TO OWN ACCURACY (not raw confidence): Agent's diagnosis is that Owen's stated confidence is HIGH while his actual accuracy is LOW (~25%), i.e. a large gap between confidence and performance / he does not realize he is getting items wrong. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the answer ties the problem to the MISMATCH between Owen's confidence and his OWN low accuracy (wording may vary: 'overconfident', 'confidence far exceeds his ~25% accuracy', 'thinks he's right when he's wrong', 'cannot tell which answers are wrong'). FAIL if the answer flags Owen for merely 'having high confidence' WITHOUT referencing that his accuracy is low / the confidence-accuracy gap, or if it flags him for low accuracy alone without the overconfidence. FAIL if it instead describes Owen as underconfident.

SHORTCUT-PROOF CONTRAST (confidence != competence): Agent demonstrates it did NOT treat confidence as competence — it must surface that Owen's confidence is about as high as the genuinely competent student's (Maya, ~90%) yet Owen's accuracy is far lower, OR that Priya is highly accurate (~85%) despite LOW confidence (~40%), so confidence level by itself does not indicate who is competent. EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent explicitly separates confidence from competence using at least one of these comparisons (Owen-high-conf-but-low-acc vs Maya, or Priya-low-conf-but-high-acc). FAIL if the agent ranks students by confidence, calls the highest-confidence student the most competent, or never distinguishes confidence from actual accuracy. FAIL if it treats Owen as 'fine' or 'confident and doing okay'.

DISTRACTOR EXCLUSION (Liam well-calibrated low scorer; Priya underconfident, large gap but harmless): Agent shows it did not confuse Owen with the other low/odd cases — it must indicate that Liam, though also low-scoring (~25%), is NOT the priority because his low confidence MATCHES his low accuracy (he is calibrated / aware he doesn't know), AND/OR that Priya, despite a large confidence-accuracy gap, is NOT the priority because her gap is UNDERconfidence on top of HIGH accuracy (the opposite, far less dangerous problem — she will not stop studying). EVALUATOR: PASS only if the agent correctly excludes at least one of Liam (low-but-calibrated) or Priya (accurate-but-underconfident) for the RIGHT reason (calibration / direction-of-error, not raw score or raw gap size). FAIL if the agent argues Liam is the priority because his score is low, treats Priya as broken in the SAME dangerous way as Owen, ranks Priya as the priority on raw miscalibration magnitude, or excludes Liam/Priya with no calibration-based reason.

INTERVENTION = METACOGNITIVE MONITORING / DIRECTED SELF-ASSESSMENT (not generic confidence-building or pure drilling): For Owen, agent prescribes support aimed at improving SELF-MONITORING / CALIBRATION via a CONCRETE external-reference mechanism — e.g. having him predict-then-check his confidence against the answer key/rubric, self-explain WHY each wrong answer was wrong, or receive structured item-level feedback so he learns to recognize his own errors. EVALUATOR: PASS only if Owen's recommended support names a concrete calibration / metacognitive-monitoring MECHANISM that puts his self-judgment up against external correctness — at least one of: predict-then-check / confidence-then-verify against an answer key or rubric, self-explanation of why answers were wrong, or structured per-item feedback tied to recognizing his own errors. FAIL if Owen's recommendation is merely the BARE WORD 'metacognition' / 'metacognitive training' / 'calibration' with NO concrete mechanism of comparing his confidence to actual correctness (vague label alone is insufficient). FAIL if the ONLY recommendation for Owen is to 'build his confidence' / encouragement (that is Priya's need), or if it is generic 'give him more practice problems' / re-teach content with NO mention of checking confidence against actual correctness or external reference. The answer must also implicitly or explicitly contrast that a different student (e.g. Priya needs confidence-building, or Liam needs content remediation) would need a DIFFERENT support, per the prompt's final request; FAIL if it prescribes the identical fix to everyone.

user_scenario.persona: Dept chair investigating instructor quality

instructions.reason_for_call: Judge evidence adequacy
instructions.task_instructions:
The CALC101 f23 midterm had n=120 students, class mean=53.9. Suppose Section A (n=60) had mean 68 and Section B (n=60) had mean 40. The department chair wants to conclude that Section B's instructor is weaker and place them on a performance improvement plan. Before endorsing this conclusion, what confounders or alternative explanations must be ruled out? What additional data should be collected? Be specific.

AUTHORITATIVE DATA SOURCE: f23_midterm_stats.json (reflects actual 120-student simulated cohort). Any discrepancies with design intent documents should defer to f23_midterm_stats.json.

nl_assertions: Agent names at least 2 distinct confounders: selection bias (which students enrolled in each section — e.g., schedule choice correlating with prior preparation), prior academic preparation differences, possible Simpson's paradox when disaggregating by subgroup, or other plausible confounders. EVALUATOR: PASS if ≥2 distinct confounders named with at least brief justification.

Agent explicitly states that the section difference alone is insufficient to attribute causation to instructor quality — i.e., acknowledges that an association ≠ causation here. EVALUATOR: PASS if agent clearly says the data are inconclusive or that causal inference requires ruling out confounders.

Agent recommends at least 1 concrete additional data source: e.g., prior GPA, pre-course placement scores, section enrollment method, or subgroup breakdowns. EVALUATOR: PASS if at least 1 specific data type is named.

user_scenario.persona: Curriculum coordinator evaluating remediation program effectiveness

instructions.reason_for_call: Evaluate causal claim about intervention
instructions.task_instructions:
In STAT201 f23, the bottom quartile of students (n=30, avg score ≈35 on the midterm where class mean was 58.6) were enrolled in a remediation workshop. On a follow-up quiz two weeks later, they averaged 48. The coordinator claims: 'The remediation works — scores jumped 13 points!' Is this conclusion justified? What statistical phenomenon could explain the improvement without any causal effect of remediation?

AUTHORITATIVE DATA SOURCE: f23_midterm_stats.json (reflects actual 120-student simulated cohort). Any discrepancies with design intent documents should defer to f23_midterm_stats.json.

nl_assertions: Agent correctly identifies regression to the mean as the primary statistical threat: students selected for extremely low scores will on average score higher on a subsequent test even without any intervention, because extreme scores partly reflect bad luck/bad day. EVALUATOR: PASS if regression to the mean is named and mechanistically explained.

Agent explains why selection on extreme scores is the key mechanism — by selecting the bottom quartile (extreme low scorers), we guarantee that random error pushed them down, so the follow-up will naturally be higher.
